utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, continue with your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday we stopped at the point when we were discussing the role of the army and the position that the army had at that time. In paragraph 85 of the Croatian part -- could you please be so kind as to find it.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: 85, you said?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It's on page 24 of that part. Because this book does not have proper pagination, it consists of different parts with different paginations.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It is stated here that there in Croatia, not to go into all the dates now, although they are totally absurd in view of the situation in Yugoslavia then, it says that there was partial occupation. Could you please explain that to me? You were there. You were following the flow of events, and you also know history. Is it possible for someone to occupy some territories where they actually live, where their homes are and the foundations of those homes were laid by their ancestors centuries ago? He wakes up one morning and somebody says that he's occupied something. You've dealt with this in theory, too, so could you please tell us?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course that's impossible, Mr. Milosevic. In all of the Republic of Croatia in 1991, there was no occupation. What was at play was a Croat separatist uprising, illegal, anti-constitutional, therefore unlawful. The only legal armed force was the Yugoslav People's Army. It is total nonsense to say there was partial occupation from the 8th of October, 1991, onwards. From the 8th of October, 1991, onwards, the Croat separatist leadership unilaterally declared independence. However, Croatia was not internationally recognised as an independent state. It was still illegal, even after the 8th of October. What was happening in Croatia was an armed conflict, but of an internal nature. Actually, a civil war caused by a separatist uprising. The Yugoslav People's Army could not have been an occupier in any part of the then still existing SFRY, Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What about the Serbs in Krajina? Could they have carried out that occupation of their own homes and their own towns and villages?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was absolutely impossible for them to carry out an occupation of their own villages, towns, homes, properties. In all those parts of Krajina the Serbs were majority population, and at the local elections they mostly won and set up a local government. The Serbs were quite simply trying to protect themselves from the newly established Ustasha regime that was already invoking the ideology and symbols of the Ustasha fascist regime from the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What about the army, since we've dealt with that subject considerably yesterday? What about the army that was in that territory for 70 years? It had its garrisons, barracks, and all of that. And after all, the army legitimately existed in that territory. And then in that year, 1991, they were encircled in their barracks and exposed to certain pressure all the way up to killings. Could they have been treated as an occupier? What did they come there? They came there 70 years ago consisting of members of different ethnicities from all over Yugoslavia and all of a sudden --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you're combining question with comment. Put your question directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So, generally speaking, in view of its status, could the army have been an occupier, and specifically in 1991 in view of the events that had to do with it could it have been an occupier?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely it could not have been an occupier. I've already said that it was the only legal armed force, and the military security service presented to the public in a documented fashion, it was all over television as far back as January 1991, that is to say, information about the illegal arming of Croatian paramilitary formations, particularly the so-called National Guards Corps, the ZNG. Enormous quantities of weapons were coming in through Hungary. To a lesser extent, the arms were Hungarian made, and mostly they were from the warehouses of the former East Germany. The German government wanted as urgently as possible to get rid of all of that, so it came as a welcome development to them to arm their Croat allies in this way. There is detailed testimony to that effect by the Croatian general Martin Spegelj who was before that commander -- a general of the Yugoslav People's Army, then commander of the Zagreb district, and then in Croatia --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj. Mr. Seselj, thank you. Mr. Seselj, I wanted to ask you whether your only reason for saying that there was no occupation after the 8th of October, 1991 is that you do not recognise Croatian independence on that day.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are saying that I do not recognise it? No one in the world recognised Croatia's independence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm asking if that is the reason.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the reason, but not the only one. Yugoslavia still existed as an internationally recognised state. Not even the secession of Slovenia had been recognised by then, although the JNA had on the basis of an agreement withdrawn from Slovenia. The former Yugoslavia still existed at the time. It was a subject of international law. It was a member of the United Nations, and no one in the world brought into question its territorial integrity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, I suggest to you in relation to this answer to read paragraph 110 now. That's only a few pages onwards. Paragraph 110.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is stated here openly: "The SFRY existed as a sovereign state until the 27th of April, 1992, when the constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was adopted replacing the constitution of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia of 1974." That is openly admitted here in the indictment. The proclamation of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was preceded by the international legal recognition although in an unlawful way of Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, and Macedonia. Why do I say in an unlawful way? According to international law, the independence of newly created states could not have been recognised in territories that were not under the control of the central government. Croatia was recognised, first of all by the Vatican and Germany and then all the other Western powers as an independent state although the central government in Zagreb did not control even a third of the territory of the -- of the Croatian territory. Two-thirds were controlled by.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, very soon Mr. Nice will be on his feet making the point that you are not here as a legal expert, because if you are here as an expert, then notice would have had to be begin of your testimony. So although you're a lawyer and a professor, bear that in mind. These are thorny legal issues that the Chamber will have to deal with. You're here as a witness as to facts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I am testifying about facts only, but along with those facts I have to give a certain explanation. You know, I'm not an illiterate or semi-literate witness here who is just guessing. I base my facts that I present on the real situation and on law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I have given you a certain leeway. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I assume that this cautioning of yours does not pertain to the fact that Mr. Seselj just read out paragraph 110 in which the other side wrote that the SFRY existed as a sovereign state until the 27th of April, 1992. Would that be a fact that they would challenge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. I have taken note of that. I'm merely speaking as to the capacity in which he's testifying here. Please continue with the examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What did they recognise? You can see that better if you open paragraphs 89 and 90. I'm going to ask you kindly to read out both, because that's what they wrote before they were ordered to issue an indictment for Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. Please read out paragraphs 89 and 90.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: For all the time that this indictment pertains to?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, no. The Kosovo indictment.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see. Towards the end of June 1991, the SFRY began to disintegrate in a succession of wars fought in the Republic of Slovenia, hereinafter Slovenia, the Republic of Croatia, hereinafter Croatia, and Bosnia-Herzegovina. On the 25th of June, 1991, Slovenia declared its independence from the SFRY which lead to the outbreak of war. A peace agreement was reached on the 8th of July, 1991. Croatia declared its independence on the 25th of June, 1991, leading to fighting between Croatian military forces on the one side and the JNA, paramilitary units, and the army of Republika Srpska Krajina on the other. On the 6th of March, 1992, Bosnia-Herzegovina declared its independence resulting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm stopping you. You're reading paragraphs 89 and 90.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is the Kosovo indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Oh, the Kosovo indictment. You have gone back to Kosovo now. And it's not for you to read out the indictment, Mr. Milosevic. Make a summary and put your question based on a summary of the paragraphs. We know the witness is literate and that he can read. There is no need for him to read it out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He can write, too, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. I take that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Seselj, this is a document of theirs where they're presenting accusations regarding Kosovo. But have you noticed that these paragraphs pertain to Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Have you seen that?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it is said here quite decidedly, I mean this indictment was written before they had received orders to issue an indictment for Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, so they did not know that they would have to do that. Croatia proclaimed its independence --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... engaged in any of these points the accused is trying to make. They plainly have nothing to do with this witness. I invite the Chamber to compel the witness to get on with evidence of facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let me hear the question you're putting, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So in paragraph 89, it says that the declaration of independence led to war, and in 90 they say for Bosnia-Herzegovina that the declaration of independence led to an all-out war. Now I'm asking you the following: What was written here pertains to Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And that's the -- there's an allegation, you say, that the declaration of independence led to war. That's a question of fact. What is the question that you wish to put to Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Both. I want to ask him whether it is possible if others create war, whether it is possible to speak of a criminal enterprise on the part of anyone in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. I'm not allowing that. That's just wholly speculative and not a proper question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a minute, Mr. Robinson. How can the Serbs attain some objectives or carry out some plans through wars created by others? That is a perfectly legitimate question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's an argument for you to present in your closing address. That's not matter for the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, paragraph 22 of this part about Croatia, and I think it's also part 22 -- or paragraph 22 of the Bosnian part, exclusively pertains to Mr. Seselj. He, as they say in paragraph 9 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: 22? Haven't you dealt with the question of Mr. Seselj providing assistance to Serb volunteers?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, let us just get this clear. It has to do with joint criminal enterprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 9, Mr. Seselj, please look at the other part --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Of the --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Croatian part, the Croatian part.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It says before that that I was this joint criminal enterprise, and then it says: "Each participant or co-perpetrator within the joint criminal enterprise played his own role or roles that significantly contributed to the overall objective of the enterprise. The roles of the participants or co-perpetrators include but are not limited to the following," and then -- and all these names are mentioned, and then in paragraph 22 we see your name, Vojislav Seselj. So you're included in this joint criminal enterprise, and that's why I'm asking you what I asked you a few moments ago. When others create war, then you are engaged in a joint criminal enterprise that was headed by me. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I've already ruled on that question. You must proceed with another question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll move on. I'll move on to another question, but I'm going to quote paragraph 22 again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: These epithets --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: To what effect are you quoting it again? It's there in front of us. If you have a specific question to put, put it and let's get on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, because I think that Mr. Seselj should answer questions that have to do with Mr. Nice's favourite topic, and some others, too, those that have to do with the Greater Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, these volunteers that they mention here commonly known as Chetniks, Seselj's men, et cetera, we clarified that yesterday concerning volunteers and their status. And then the last sentence in paragraph 22 reads as follows: "In addition, he openly espoused and encouraged creation of a Greater Serbia by violence and other unlawful means and actively participated in war propaganda and spreading interethnic hatred." So directly in these accusations levelled against me here you are mentioned as a participant in a joint criminal enterprise. Now I wish to ask you about this violence, these unlawful means through which you endeavoured to create a Greater Serbia and about the spread of national hatred. In order to get a clear explanation, let us see how much this has to do with real facts, what is written here.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only one thing is a fact here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There's no question there in my opinion. Yesterday Mr. Seselj made it abundantly clear that he did espouse the concept of a Greater Serbia but certainly not by violent or any other unlawful means. This matter has been dealt with over and over again in the course of the evidence so far of this witness, and there was no question there and the whole point seems to me simply to be an exercise in making submissions which will be -- and the stage for which will be reached much later in the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Move on to another question, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I will ask specific questions dealing with this, and they deserve an explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Seselj, you openly advocated the concept of Greater Serbia, and your newspaper, the newspaper of your party, as we have seen from previous quotations, is called Greater Serbia. What kind of idea is that?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a ideological concept, and it was first mentioned in public all the way back in 1683 when the Turks were defeated. Djordje Brankovic, a prominent leader from that time, addressed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why don't we find out what Mr. Seselj thinks about the Greater Serbia rather than a 16th century or 17th century concept?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy, I understand the concept of Greater Serbia as it was originally understood and designed in the 17th century. However, in many trials that took place before The Hague Tribunal, and I must say I read most of the judgements, many witnesses, illiterate and semi-literate, speak of Greater Serbia without knowing what it means. And in the judgements later, their words are taken unquestioningly. I, as a leading nationalist and ideologist of today and a scholar can give you the original meaning of the concept of Greater Serbia, and I think it would be useful for this trial and other trials conducted here as well. Nobody here, none of those accused of taking part in the joint criminal enterprise never worked for a Greater Serbia. It never crossed their mind. Something that I held as a personal view is being ascribed in this indictment to other people who had nothing to do with it. Now, let me explain what the idea means, what the concept of Greater Serbia actually means. And I will try to be brief and very concise, whenever I deal with some historical ideas and concepts. But I would really like to explain this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what you've said so far, that you held something as a personal view about Greater Serbia, and that's what we want to hear. We don't want to know the detail of how that evolved, unless it becomes relevant as a result of what you say about your own personal understanding of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I was going to add this point: The question of Greater Serbia was touched upon in the opening only insofar as it fell from the mouths of others, including this man. It appears in the way we've already seen in the Croatian indictment. It was touched upon, I think, in the background historical evidence to the extent thought necessary by the Prosecution. It was substantially enlarged upon by witnesses either listed as and called as experts or as factual witnesses in the accused's case, and Chamber will have in mind both Mihailovics, Avramov, Popov, Terzic. There is no need for further alleged expertise certainly coming from a witness who hasn't served a report, and I respectfully adopt the position proposed by His Honour Judge Bonomy.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, just let me draw your attention to one fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Chamber is consulting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, we'll hear you on in concept of Greater Serbia. It may be necessary, as you say, to delve into the history, but do that very briefly. Come to the modern-day concept and let us know what you understood the Greater Serbia concept to mean. So very briefly now let's hear it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The concept --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You are not to interrupt. I have asked the witness a question, and I'm allowed to. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I have a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I am stopping you. I've stopped you. Mr. Seselj, I've asked you a question. Answer it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The concept of Greater Serbia implies a unified Serbian state including all Serbian lands where Serbs are a majority population. However, it is opposed to century-long Vatican, Austrian and other attempts to reduce the Serbian people only to members of the Orthodox Christian religion because the Serbian people in its ethnic being includes Orthodox, Catholic, and Muslim Serbs equally. Djordje Brankovic, when he dealt with the Austrian emperor, when the Austrian army was advancing against the Turks and freed many Serbian lands, so Djordje Brankovic asked about those Serbian lands. And what is defined as a Serbian land, where Serbian language is spoken. He asked from the Austrian emperor that all these Serbian lands become a special unit within the Empire, and the Austrian emperor accepted this request, appointed him a count, gave him the title, and made him governor of Banat and some other lands. So when Austria freed many of those lands, it suddenly became frightened of the idea, because the Serbs occupied a great part of the Balkan, and Djordje Brankovic was exiled to Hebar, and actually limited to that area. He was being kept, provided for, but not allowed to leave. In 1983, Arsenije Gagovic asked for Russian help to free the Serbian land from Turkish yoke and then Austrian yoke. That is when the concept is written about for the second time. And the third mention of that concept dates back to the first great uprising against the Turks in 1844. So that is basically a freedom-loving idea, the idea of being liberated from the Turkish yoke in which we lived for five centuries, from the Austrian yoke in which we also lives for centuries, and then the Venetian yoke as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let me summarise, then, the concept as you said. The unified Serbian state with all Serbian lands where Serbs are a majority population, and that includes Orthodox, Catholic, and Muslim Serbs equally, and that is in contradistinction to the century-long Vatican position. That's clear. Mr. Nice, I didn't -- I ---let me -- I didn't --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't explain to you the key details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, are you saying it's not an important part of the Prosecution case?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We have always been careful in the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's the main basis on which the three indictments are joined. The main basis in the appeals judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The difference between the concept of all Serbs living in one state, the accused's notion, and the historical concept of Greater Serbia about which we've heard a very great deal and about which great argue may or may not validly be heard in this court, and we've always accepted that the accused has either never used the words Greater Serbia himself or has only ever used them in attribution to others but that others such as this man have used the term, and we've always distinguished - and if you look at my opening you'll find this - between the words used by others and our case which is that this accused was motivated by the desire to have all Serbs live in one state, in part. If he wasn't motivated by that he was motivated by other objectives that were personal to him that built upon that particular concept. Now, it may be at the end of the day that there is little or no difference between the practical realities of one and another, but one is definitely a term of historical art and is not one that we have -- at least not one that I have used specifically in respect of this accused, and I've always been very cautious about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, I have one question about your definition. Included within that description you said: "And what is defined as a Serbian land, where Serbian language is spoken." Now, did you mean to say that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you not claim that Croats spoke Serbian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So Serbian lands in this definition includes what, the whole of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Well, I'm confused, you see, about that description. Nothing to do with history --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, again, you gave more time to Mr. Nice than to me, whereas I'm the one testifying about it. I really wish to explain and I really will be brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You said something that I would like you to clarify. Now, what is the extent to which the Serbian language is spoken according to your understanding of this definition of this Greater Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. An overwhelming majority of today's Croats are Serb Catholics, Catholic Serbs. All Muslims in Bosnia and Herzegovina and the area of Raska are Muslim Serbs, whereas the concept of Croat had three ethnic meanings through history. The first Croats were a people of Western Slav origin, close to Poles and Czechs. They inhabited the Balkans between Gvozd and the Adriatic Sea. They had their own language which was called Cakavski in linguistics. It was a small territory, and in the 11th century it reached up to the Vrbas River. I suppose you know it's a river flowing through Banja Luka. It was under the Croatian King Petar Kresimir. That population that later became scattered deep into Europe against the advance of the Turks, they were Catholics, and they ran away before the Turks. You have such Croats nowadays in Gradiska, in Austria, in Czechoslovakia, et cetera. They are the real Croats. When Croatia fell under the Turkish yoke almost completely, then the Hungarian king moved part of the Croats to Slavonia. Slavonia was inhabited by Carpathians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you just answer the question, which is the extent to which the Serbian language is spoken. That means today or at the time of the conflict, rather, according to your definition of this Greater Serbia. Why can't you just tell me that? That's the fact I'd like to know about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Serbian language was spoken in Serbia, the entire Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro, and almost the entire Croatia, except for three districts, Zagreb, Krizevci and Varazdin. That is in the west of today's Croatia. In the 19th century on the orders of the Vatican and the Viennese court, all Croats accepted Serbian as their own language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If someone else wants to explore it they may well do so. I don't want to know that at this stage. I want to get the definition clear at the time. So you're saying that the Greater Serbia would include the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Montenegro, and almost all Croatia is subject to the three districts about which you were explaining the historical origins of the languages spoken there. Is that the position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I want to do here is that let you know that the concept of Greater Serbia can by no means be identified with any sort of practice of persecuting Catholic, Muslim, or any other population. In all the proclamations of the freedom-loving Serbian movement, the Serbian Radical Party, and all other parties I've led, we keep appealing for the unification of Protestant, Catholic, Orthodox, Muslim, and all other Serbs. That cannot be linked with the concept of Greater Serbia. Persecution is not in line with the concept of Greater Serbia, but you won't let me say it. That's why we insist on including Catholics, Protestants, Muslims into our party and giving them high positions. We are opposing the Vatican policy that appeals to Catholics to declare themselves as Catholics, non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj has to slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The interpreters have asked you to slow down. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. But I believe I am -- you have expressed the position now, that the concept of Greater Serbia is inherently inconsistent with persecutions of Muslims or any other -- any other sect.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to tell you one more thing very briefly, please, Mr. Robinson. All these people that are mentioned here as members, participants in the joint criminal enterprise, we're against the secession of Slovenia. I was the only one who was in favour of the secession of Slovenia, if the Slovenes wanted. I had made several public appearances on Slovene TV supporting them. But I was against the secession of Croatia because I knew that it was the same people who was about to secede. We were one and the same people. Even those who are not real authentic Serbs in those three districts have been through intermarriage integrated. If you look at Serbs, Muslims, Catholics, and Croats, you cannot find any difference between us except for religion. If you have any conflict between the accused --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I did have a matter to raise, and it is over this troubling issue of Greater Serbia and how far or whether it is relevant to the Prosecution's case, because in opening, Mr. Nice has dealt with one part of his opening address to the Court, but there was another passage which I have here on the first day, and it reads thus: "The army, the evidence will be, was no better, it having committed itself to the accused's programme. Officers being instilled with the ideology of brotherhood and unity totally abandoned everything in favour of a Greater Serbia. They shared the arrogance, did the army, of the civilian leaders and saw no reason to confer." It did seem that the thrust of the Prosecution case was that there had been a plan by this accused for a Greater Serbia, and there has been cross-examination to that effect. And the accused has to know what he's got to deal with in relation to his case and how to apportion his time. So if concessions are going to be made on the issue, they must be made clearly and frankly and transparently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I am fully in agreement with you, Mr. Kay, and I'm going to ask Mr. Nice now if his position is different, then say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My position has never been different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Because I had the clear impression that this was an essential foundation of the Prosecution's case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm very sorry about that, because I think Mr. Kay's quotation, by the way, doesn't deal with the fact that what he's citing from is my citation from a witness. Now, I have always made it plain -- and at the moment I've got in front of me the joinder arguments as well. You'll find it quite helpful to go through them electronically, pick up the word "greater" and see who refers to Greater Serbia. The accused does. What I cannot do is deny witnesses who we call their right to express their opinions on the matter, but what I always made plain - and I've made it plain through all the expert witnesses that have been called and that I've cross-examined - that the words "Greater Serbia" come from others and not from the accused. What we allege against the accused is that he cleaved to - for his own purposes maybe - a plan to have all Serbs living in one state. That creates a de facto Greater Serbia because the western boundaries, Virovitica-Karlobag line are all the same. But are we saying that he is a proponent personally of an historical Greater Serbia concept? We haven't said that. And that distinction is one I've always made, because I've recognise that the accused doesn't use these words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But you're not saying it was one of the basic foundations that one of the basic ideas prompting the joint criminal enterprise?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The concept that all Serbs should live in one state is different from the concept of a Greater Serbia as you've just heard from this witness who has given you a great historical overview from his perspective of what Greater Serbia is all about. It's different. As I've already said, it may in fact have little practical difference, but if this Chamber's going to understand both the history and the accused's behaviour and motivation during the conflict, it will need to deal with the fact that there is a historical concept to a Greater Serbia to which he never associated himself or read, as far as I can see, never, with his taking power. Maybe with his being put in the driving seat of movements of others that did espouse Greater Serbia he pursued policies that may have had a similar effect. But have we ever said that that was his driving force, the historical concept of a Greater Serbia; no, we haven't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So if I understand you, Mr. Nice, the Prosecution's approach is more -- it's more pragmatic. It's more empirical.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Absolutely. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You're concentrating more on the idea of all Serbs living in one state.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Correct. And of course, let there be no doubt about it, our case has always been that for a person who could have that as his driving force there might have been good reason for him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- allowing the influence of people such as this witness who espoused quite specifically a Greater Serbia, but that's different. Did he use the words himself, no. Incidentally I made one slip of the tongue when I was identifying the witnesses who have dealt with this and to whom you may wish to turn, not least to see what my cross-examination on the point is. I made that mistake of eliding names that are both surnames and first names. It's Kosta Mihailovic and Mihailo Markovic, who are two of the witnesses. I said there were two people with the same surname. I'll just check if there's anything else I should --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, please do not allow Mr. Nice to insult me. I was never under the control of Mr. Milosevic, and Mr. Milosevic never made it possible for me to do anything in political life. I did nothing that I did not achieve by my own efforts. So this is an insult to me. In this indictment I am being linked to this joint criminal enterprise, the alleged criminal enterprise, based on my idea of the Greater Serbia and I'm being put together with my ideological opponents, among which was Mr. Milosevic. We had only one thing in common at the beginning of the war and that was that none of us agreed to the unilateral secession of Croatia without negotiations and without an agreement. We had nothing else in common, and I insist on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, can I ask you, how you understand the difference of the Greater Serbia idea and the idea of one -- all Serbs living in one state. How do you understand?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, first of all one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you not saying that it is saying the same thing in the --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- at the end of the day?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At the end it may be that the accused's aim was for that which could qualify as a de facto Greater Serbia, yes. Did he -- did he find the source of his position, for I don't wish to identify it as an ideology or a platform. Did he find the source of his position at least overtly in historical concept of Greater Serbia; no, he didn't. His was perhaps to borrow His Honour Judge Robinson's term or was stated to be the pragmatic one of ensuring that all the Serbs who had lived in the former Yugoslavia should be allowed for either constitutional or other reasons to live in the same unit. That meant as we know historically from his perspective first of all that the former Yugoslavia shouldn't be broken up because he argued, well, then, if they all live in the same place one where they can do it in the former Yugoslavia. Once the former Yugoslavia breaks up, the Prosecution case is the only way you can achieve the desire that all Serbs should live in the same state is by doing the various things that happened in the three different territories. Now, -- or in particular in the two different territories of Croatia and Bosnia. So that that's why we describe it as -- or we don't describe it. We analyse it in the terms of his desire or his expressed desire that all Serbs should live in one state, accepting that at the end of the exercise the factual position may be little different from that which would have been wanted by this particular witness under his long-term historical concept of Greater Serbia. The Court will remember with the various witnesses we've had how we've been able to look at historical maps and indeed how we've heard the accused referring back to historical maps, such as the map of the London conference, or the maps that were generated after the Second World War, and try and draw support on those ideas to justify in more contemporary negotiations his position. But his position, it appears from the evidence about him, was not built on that concept itself, not with the emotions and maybe the philosophy or whatever else, that this witness would rely on. It was on more pragmatic grounds. Now, I'm sorry if that hasn't become clear, but it's been absolutely at the forefront of my examination and cross-examination of witnesses. And I go back to what Mr. Kay said. If you look at the opening, you will see that the word only appears from me in the mouths of others and that we were careful then and in the argument about joinder to express things much more carefully so far as this accused is concerned. And indeed I was going to raise this point yesterday when the accused mischaracterised our presentation or my presentation by saying that there was a leitmotif of Greater Serbia as against him because there never was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, the passage cited to me by me said "the evidence will be," which indicates the evidence to be relied upon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It may be, Mr. Nice, as you say, that there is no essential difference, but for my part I'd like -- I'm going to have my Chamber staff look at the evidence and see whether it bears out the points that you have -- that you have made, because if -- it's important to ascertain whether it was or was not a part of the Prosecution's case. Mr. Milosevic. In fact, I remember in the Rule 98 bis no-case motion, I remember the Chamber dealing with that as --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We better look at those filings as well then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- dealing with that as one part of the Prosecution case, and looking at evidence which might have supported it. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, for the duration of 15 minutes here Mr. Nice has been explaining that I did not advocate a Greater Serbia and then that I did advocate a Greater Serbia. I don't see how it is possible to have a coherent conversation if one doesn't know what the accusations are. He is now talking about the historical idea and separating out from the non-historical idea and so on. At the beginning, before a single witness was brought, Mr. Nice did not deal with any historical concepts. What he did was present vague and incredible nebulous arguments. Then he said that through witnesses he would show what the accused did. Look at this logical caricature presented by Mr. Nice just awhile ago. On the one hand, he admits what I am saying, and that is that the thesis of all Serbs in one state can be implemented through Yugoslavia, which is why we advocated the preservation of Yugoslavia since it was an existing state in which all the Serbs lived in one state. Then he goes on that in three different places, and he's referring to the three parts of this alleged indictment, wanted to implement this in various ways. These were three separatist movements breaking up Yugoslavia. If this hasn't become clear to you by now, then nothing is clear to you. I did not organise these three separatist movements in Croatia, Bosnia, and Kosovo in order to create a Yugoslavia in which all Serbs could live in one state when Yugoslavia has been existing for 70 years. Is there any logic in this? This is insulting to the average intelligence of an average man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic. Let's proceed now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that Mr. Nice should pull himself together before I go on and recall what he's accusing me of so that I can put questions to the witness. I mean, about a Greater Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Proceed, Mr. Milosevic. Mr. Nice has made his points.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Actually --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There's no need to hear him any further on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, with your leave, in light of the observations that have been made and the concern of the Court, I would invite you just to -- I'll just find it for you in the -- because it's -- actually encapsulates the position right from the beginning. If you'll just give me one second. It's in the opening, and -- what I said was this dealing with western Slavonia. I think it's on about page 50. "The creed openly espoused by the man Seselj went by the title of Greater Serbia. It's a phrase that is bound to be heard in this Court. We will not ourselves encourage its excessive use for the fear that our shorthand may lead to a brevity of thinking. We don't particularly associate it as a title with the" --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not getting the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us have that technical matter attended to, Mr. Nice. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The creed openly espoused by the man Seselj went by the title of Greater Serbia. It's a phrase that is bound to be heard in this Court. We will not ourselves encourage its excessive use for fear that our shorthand may lead to a brevity of thinking. We don't particularly associate it as a title with the approach of the accused whose purposes we have already separately described. That he might rely on the support of people who had perhaps extreme nationalist views going by particular titles is, again, for reasons already given, not surprising." Now, that I think is the first time in the opening that the words "Greater Serbia" featured on my lips, and if you go back to the joinder motion it featured on the lips of the accused and not I think until reply Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. from me. So that's always been our position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In response to the comment that I just made that I would have the Chamber staff research it, I've just been handed a copy of the section of the 98 bis decision, paragraph 249, which refers to Ambassador Galbraith testifying that he believed that the accused, and here I quote: "Was the architect of a policy of creating Greater Serbia and that little happened without his knowledge and involvement." And then in paragraph 288 the Chamber identifies seven bases for its conclusion that the Chamber could infer that the accused not only knew of the genocidal plan but that he also shared with its members the intent to destroy. And this second matter referred to is the accused's advocacy of and support for the concept of a Greater Serbia. I think that was the reference that I had in mind to the 98 bis.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] The same way as I can't confine and shouldn't rehearse and don't rehearse witnesses away from their use of terminology that may not be our use. I have already made our position clear, and I don't think you'll find - but I live to be corrected - in our 98 submissions that we expressed ourselves differently or inconsistently from the way we had throughout.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's an important clarification to make, Mr. Nice, that the Prosecution's case is not so attached -- is not as attached to the concept of a Greater Serbia as it is to the idea of all Serbs living in the same land.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In one state. In one state. Although I would have to say that I still have it -- I still have a doubt as to whether there isn't a proper basis for saying that that was the Prosecution's case. Yes. Initially at any rate. Mr. Milosevic, yes. Just please ask --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... let us move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, you are a professor at the Faculty of Law. You have a Ph.D.. As I don't understand Mr. Nice's position, can you tell me whether you understand it?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Seselj, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's not a proper question for Mr. Seselj. Mr. Nice has explained his position. Let us -- let us move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But Mr. Robinson --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It is an authoritative statement of the Prosecution's position. It comes from the -- from the officer who is the Chief Prosecutor in this case.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Allow me, Mr. Robinson, to say that my meager intellectual faculties are insufficient for me to understand what Mr. Nice has said. I wish to have it explained to me whether the existence of Yugoslavia for 70 years in which all Serbs, Croats, and the Slav Muslims lived, whether my advocation of the preservation of this Yugoslavia or the historical concept that was not spoken of, what it is actually that Mr. Nice is alleging against me. He is using concepts he does not understand, and you don't understand what he is saying and neither do I. This is utter confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's not a matter for you to say. It's quite out of order for you to suggest that the Chamber does not understand what Mr. Nice said. We understand what he has said, and I take it to be a very important statement on the part of the Prosecutor, because we have to know the basis on which the Prosecution is proceeding. So proceed with your next question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a good thing that after three years you are supposed to see what the basis of the Prosecution is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, in tab 4 there is a part, a small part, a small excerpt from your book. You're the author. In all fairness, this is from the second edition.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no difference between the first and second editions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, there isn't but I'd like to draw your attention to that after all. It shows that your book sold very well if a second edition was published. It is called "The Ideology of Serbian Nationalism," written by you. In relation to that, I wish to put a few questions to you. Let me just see what the page is. 980. It's a rather poor copy, the one I have. So on page 980, and this part that we've made an excerpt of was translated into English too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I remind you of your duty to ensure that the Trial Chamber has before it the passage to which you are referring.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When was the first edition published?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first edition was published also in 1992, but before that a shorter version of that book was published in 1998. I worked on that, and I supplemented the book.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The witness said 1998.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is my monograph based on the scholarly work of Professor Dr. Lazar Kostic, a renowned university professor at the time of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia and one of the leading Serb anti-communist emigres after the Second World War. He wrote a total of 84 books. I first dealt with his scholarly work, and then on the basis of his scholarly work I developed other theses and assumptions. And of course I supplemented my work with areas that Professor Kostic had not dealt with. That constitutes the most all-embracing, synthetic work on the ideology of Serbian nationalism to date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's on page 3 in the second paragraph in the English translation, what I wish to cite to Mr. Seselj. So on page 980, you say: "The Serbs through" --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: What did you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Page 980. I'm quoting part of the text. "The Serbs through the strength of their own spirit liberated parts of their own people and national territories. The pan Serbian agenda is not a figment of the imagination of a handful of daydreamers. It was imposed on politicians by history and ethnography. It stems from the consciousness of a nation which has strived for several centuries and through constant and unanimous efforts to merge its people's destinies." Before that, in the preceding paragraph, I'm going to deal with that very briefly, you talk about Denis' analysis of the nature of Serb nationalism, and it says that this stems from the desire for happiness that everybody carries within themselves and which is interlinked with the need for the full development of our effective capacities." So -- or actually let me just finish with Denis and then I'm going to ask you for further explanations. Just one more paragraph, the last one before the second or, rather, other chapter, speaking of the Serbs. Their quarrels were used by the Hungarians and Germans whose interest was for the Serbs to have the biggest possible mistakes. Their enemies did not see or did not want to see the higher qualities of the Serbian people, their resilience acquired in difficult times, the refinement and sharpness of their intelligence, particularly the determination of their idealism and the strength of their will which have endured in spite of many visible oscillations. Winds disturb a river's surface but do not change its course." What you speak about here is a work that considerably preceded all these events, and this is based on the work of an analyst who took into account the main points that this dealt with. Tell us to what extent this matched your own thoughts on the matter and to what extent did you contribute to the affirmation of this idea on the plane of theory? I wish to remind you that the title of the book is "The Ideology of Serbian Nationalism."

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: On three pages I deal with Ernest Denis' book that is called "Greater Serbia." It was published in Paris in 1915 during the time of the First World War. Ernest Denis is fascinated by the efforts made by the Serbian people and their two great victories over the Austro-Hungarian army at Cer and Kolubara in 1914 which made all of Europe admire them. Ernest Denis concludes that they -- that everybody in the world should recognise the will and wish of the Serb people to unite.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is the relevance of this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the extent to which this can be seen, namely, what existed during the times of the First World War and what existed in the time that we are discussing here, 1991 and 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Seselj --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. Milosevic, I've cut you off because the proper course is for you to answer my question that I have asked and then await my ruling. You don't proceed with Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You have not explained the relevance sufficiently, but I'll give you another try to explain the relevance. Otherwise, I'm not allowing the question. We need to move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Let's give it a very pragmatic angle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, as for what it says here in your book, as for what you wrote yourself and as for what you presented by way of the views of other scholars, in this programme, this programme of a Greater Serbia seen through your own eyes, seen through the eyes of foreign scholars, does it mean the subordination of the Croats?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. What I deal with here is the presentation of arguments about the Serb origins, about their ethnic substrate and curbing the Vatican and previously Austro-Hungarian ideology that forced Serb Catholics to declare themselves as Croats. In the 19th century, the Croatian national awareness was only limited to Zagreb, Varazdin and Krizevci, those districts. There are many historical testimonials that they consider themselves to be Serbs. Bosnian Catholics consider them to be Serbs. Friar Grga Matic, a Catholic priest, is writing Serbian nationalist poems with great delight. I am indicating these historical examples, this awareness of single origins and a single nation that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I've stopped you because I'm going to consult with my colleagues, and I'll also hear Mr. Kay on this point as to whether in light of the statement made by the Prosecutor we need to hear more evidence on this concept. The Prosecutor said that his case is concerned more with the idea of all Serbs living in the same state than with the concept of a Greater Serbia. I don't think that that necessarily means that all evidence on Greater Serbia is to be excluded, but certainly it should be taken into account. I'll consult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, do you --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, I can't see any basis of taking this further myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber's position is this: We'll not exclude automatically all evidence on the concept of a Greater Serbia on the basis of the Prosecutor's statement made some minutes ago. But this particular piece of evidence being given by Mr. Seselj, we don't find particularly helpful. So move on to another area, Mr. Milosevic. We have heard a lot about -- we have heard a lot about the history.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, there is another link there. In his approach, Mr. Nice equals the fact that in Yugoslavia all Serbs lived in one state with a Greater Serbia. He's actually proclaiming Yugoslavia to be a Greater Serbia. All Serbs in one state is not an idea. It is a statement of fact. That was the case for 70 years, for the duration of Yugoslavia. For 70 years, all Serbs lived in one state. That was a fact of life. It's a material fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's precisely because of the possible interchangeability of the two ideas, Greater Serbia and all Serbs living in the same state, it's precisely because of that that I've said that the Chamber will not rule evidence -- rule out evidence on this matter. We can't rule it out in that way. But the evidence which Mr. Seselj is giving now we don't find helpful. So move on to -- you can deal with the concept, but let us deal with -- with the matters that are more relevant to the indictment so far as the idea either of a Greater Serbia or of all Serbs living in the same state.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm going to give -- the Chamber will give further consideration to the significance that is to be attached to the statement made by the Prosecutor, and he'll ask Mr. Kay to bear this in mind. I've just --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I've just been handed another part of the Chamber's decision on the no-case submission -- oh, this is the submission itself. This is the submission itself from the Prosecution -- from the -- this is the Prosecution's response. In paragraph 262 of the Prosecutor's response it says: "This amounted de facto to planning for a Greater Serbia." That seems plain enough. "There was not a single fully articulated plan from the outset and the plan changed with the changing circumstances," et cetera. And then in paragraph 273, in the middle of that paragraph: "However, the self-determination of the Serbian people would include the territories with Serb majorities in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, including a de facto Greater Serbia -- achieving a de facto Greater Serbia, a term he always avoided using in public or at all." That's closer to what Mr. Nice explained in court some minutes ago, the more pragmatic approach. And in paragraph 276, the third-to-last line: "More generally, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. witnesses were clear that the accused wanted to create a Greater Serbia." So, Mr. Nice, I give you my personal view. I don't think we have settled the matter. Clearly it's an important matter to be settled. As Mr. Kay said very importantly, the accused needs to know the case that he's facing, and if there has been what I term advisedly a retreat from a particular position, then we need to know that. And if the present position is in substance the same as the concept of a Greater Serbia, then of course we still need to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, our position has in no way changed. There's no question of a retreat or change of position. I'm grateful that you've located the passages on the submission that I myself have been reviewing, and indeed the only other passage I think which you may find helpful - and I'll just turn it up for you; I had a little bit before but I can find it easily enough - Is in the joinder application to which you earlier referred and we can look at that. As I explained, if we go to the beginning of this hearing before His Honour Judge Jorda and other Judges, what happened, rather, in the sort of straw man way, I think, was that the accused, let's find it, made many references or several references about Greater Serbia. They were picked up by Mr. Kay -- the accused also made references to Greater Albania and all sorts of other historical concepts of that kind. I think that when it came to my reply, which is the first time I think if at all that I mention Greater Serbia - I'll just try to find it for you - Mr. Tapuskovic as he was then with us made some observations again about Greater Serbia. His Honour Judge Hunt raised the issue of the Greater Serbia argument with Mr. Kay. There was a certain amount of discussion between them. But I think my only reference to it, and I think I've found it. I'll just check that it's me. I'm sure it is. Yes, it's on page 80 of the transcript or thereabouts, 81, I think. And I said this: "Greater Serbia features, of course, in the writing and it features only to a very limited extent in the pleadings. Features, for example, in one of the indictments in the mouth of Seselj, his rabble-rousing words. It features in another of the indictments as being something that was being advocated at the same time as the accused was doing, that which he is said to have done, and it features in the third indictment as being a way of looking at things but always qualified in the way that I qualified it," and the transcript reads on the last occasion when this -- and then I -- and that must be, I think, a reference, although incompletely captured on the transcript, to the way I'd expressed our position about the accused, right at the beginning without ever using the term Greater Serbia. Then I go on to make this clear. "We say as we have said from the beginning that there was a common plan by this accused to retain or gain territory for the purpose of exercising power via a central Serbian state differently expressed on different occasions but to that effect." So at all times I had separated the Prosecution's position, which was to identify what the accused was actually --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My microphone is not working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, may I stop you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We have one more clear passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Another passage in our Rule 98 bis decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's paragraph 252. I will read it out the passage: "It is the Prosecution case that the accused intended to destroy the Muslim population of those parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina essentially earmarked for the inclusion into a Greater Serbia. Without that destruction, the accused's goal could not be realised," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That seems clear enough, Mr. Nice. That was the Prosecution's --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's the Chamber's interpretation of what we expressed in our submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. That's the Prosecution's response.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That the -- but, again, it's the de facto position as opposed to the historical concept. And that's always been our stated position. And if you'd permit me to read out from where I was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. And in the -- I've just been handed the -- a section of the motion for joinder. This is page 6 under the heading "Rule --" it's the -- oh, it's at page 5 of the joinder motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That I don't have before me at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. And this is what the Trial Chamber said in its --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Prosecution's.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll take the break now and come back to this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think -- I'm grateful. I think that's the last reference from me in the joinder argument. I'll come back to it after the break, if Your Honour pleases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We will adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I've had more time to consider this matter, and I am clearly of the view that the concept of a Greater Serbia was indeed a central plank in the Prosecution's case. It was the basis on which the motion for joinder was made, and I refer to two passages, paragraph 13 of the motion: "In the present case the three indictments concern the same transaction in the sense of a common scheme, strategy, or plan, namely the accused Milosevic's overall conduct in attempting to create a Greater Serbia, an centralised Serbian state encompassing the Serb populated areas of Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina and all of Kosovo." And then on page 18 -- sorry, paragraph 18, page 7, at the bottom "He, that is Milosevic, later exploited these affairs in Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina and Kosovo in order to further his campaign to create a Greater Serbia." And indeed it was for that reason that the Appeals Chamber overturned the decision of this Trial Chamber rejecting the motion for joinder, because the Trial Chamber found that there was no common thread, that the concept of a Greater Serbia was not a common thread. It was not the same transaction and the Appeals Chamber held otherwise. So I find it startling now to hear you say that it was not part of the Prosecution case. It may be that you now say, you now take a more pragmatic decision which is reflected in the idea of what Mr. Milosevic wanted and the other participants in the alleged joint criminal enterprise was that all Serbs should live in the same state, and you may want to say that that in fact amounts to Greater Serbia, but I cannot allow you to say that it was not a part of the Prosecution's case. The accused needs to know what he's facing. And if you need time to consider this matter, Mr. Nice, as I consider it extremely important to the case, then we'll give you time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I personally don't need time. There hadn't been any change, and I'm sorry that the Chamber hasn't understood the position more fully earlier. Can I take you -- I've only just been able to review --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May I say that this time will not be counted against the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May I -- I've only just been able to turn up the filings. The one that Your Honour refers to which I've looked at, and also you'll want to look probably at the interlocutory appeal filing. I haven't got the date. But I'll quote you a passage from that, or two passages. But before I do, first of all, I don't actually think there's -- there's a distinction or difference of the kind that Your Honours are apparently concerned about, because it's always been clear in the way I've expressed the case and the questions I've asked that the practical effects for which the accused sought are similar in geographical scope to the effects of the implementation of a formal Greater Serbia plan of the kind that this witness might have wanted. Second, identifying over a long -- from a long history the precise definition of something, a term of art like Greater Serbia is never going to be easy if you use it as a philosophical term going back to the 16th century as he would claim, running through Nacertanije as we've heard in evidence, reflected in practical political proposals as in the London conference, being dealt with by Moljevic on a philosophical basis and so on. It's going to be very difficult to find a precise definition if you use it as a term of art. And third, before I come to the passage to which I'm going to refer, had we ever alleged in specific terms that this accused espoused in philosophical terms Greater Serbia, it would have been probably unwise and probably wrong, because he would have been able to say the words never fell from his lips and nor they did. So that -- that's why from the minute that I was in charge of the presentation of this case, I was cautious in the extreme in way we argued for and presented his thinking processes, making it clear that his thinking processes, or at least his spoken expression of his thinking processes, would have led to a de facto position, a de facto Greater Serbia, similar in geographical extent to that which might have been argued for by this witness. And if we then go to the appeal brief, at paragraph 14 I made the following observations or we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: To the appeal brief?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's just get the date of it. I'll come back to. This is 15th of January, 2002. I'm grateful to Ms. Dicklich. And paragraph 14, I think, has the first reference where I said the following: "The Trial Chamber based its analysis on three factors which the Prosecution submits were erroneously applied. First, the Trial Chamber found that because the words 'Greater Serbia' plan did not appear in the Kosovo indictment and 'it is only in relation to other individuals that the man is mentioned in the Bosnia Croatian indictments' that the nexus was too nebulous to constitute a common scheme, strategy, or plan." Now, if we then go to the next reference to -- I'm sorry. I'll find the next reference which is on paragraph 27. We'll see how -- probably a better look at the paragraph in context. It begins with thus: "In the present case, the purpose of the joint criminal enterprise alleged in all three indictments is substantially similar," and then I set out -- or we set out in the Croatia indictment the purposes stated as follows. And we dealt with the Bosnia indictment and the Kosovo indictment, and I can quote it if you think I should do so and. Then we said this: "Although the wording differs slightly, the import of the purpose is the same to remove the majority of the non-Serb civilian population from areas which the Serbs wished to make or maintain as Serb-controlled territory. The Prosecution explained in its written submissions as well as during the hearing that the phrase 'Greater Serbia' was merely descriptive of the plan by the accused to create and maintain a centralised Serbian state," and then there is a footnote, I imagine, to the references. "Such a man which encompassed both getting rid of non-Serb civilians and attaining and maintaining Serb domination over the remaining population in that territory remained consistent throughout the time period covered by all three indictments despite the different language used. The Prosecution submits that it was an error for the Trial Chamber not to consider that the purpose as well as the plan charged in all three indictments was the same." And I think that's the last reference in that pleading to the term "Greater Serbia," at least as discovered or discoverable electronically. So that whatever may have been the understanding or misunderstanding before the Trial Chamber, the position was made quite clear to the Appeals Chamber in the written filing that we were looking at the de facto, the pragmatic position as we described it. And when you look at the oral arguments, and as I respectfully remind you, remember that it was the accused and Mr. Kay who referred to Greater Serbia, and I quite specifically identified how we were relying on it and the way in which if featured, then our position hadn't changed. And I know it hadn't changed because I've always understood our position to be that it's the express desire to have all Serbs in one state, de facto Greater Serbia if you will, co-extensive geographical extension in practical terms with what had been achieved by those specifically espousing Greater Serbia, but not the espousing by this accused vocally, who knows what was in his mind, that is to be proved in other ways and never espoused by him. And I don't think there is any difficulty in establishing in due course with questioning of this witness that his position differed from the accused's position because he espoused Greater Serbia, the philosophical concept with which we've been either troubled or enthralled in the extensive expert evidence that's been given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: His concept is different.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. It's differently based. It's historically based.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I ask -- no microphone. Can I ask you, Mr. Nice, why reference was made at all by the Prosecution to the concept of a Greater Serbia. Why were these words chosen if the Prosecution knew that they had a distinctive historical context?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, you can certainly ask the question and I can do my best to answer it. I have both the difficulties of some separation from some of the drafting as an individual and a considerable passage of time over which to look, but I -- I suspect that the proper answer would be as follows, that if you view a man, this accused, who is doing something that is very similar in its effect to but different in it's expression from those who espouse and argue for the philosophical and historical concept of Greater Serbia, you have to decide do we say he's a Greater Serbian. For the reasons I've already given that would have been unwise and indeed wrong. Do you nevertheless draw to the Court's attention that there may be significance in the existence both of the notion of Greater Serbia as expressed by others? Yes, you do. And that's why in both the Croatian and the Bosnian indictments the concept attributed to this witness is dealt with. Do you express the understanding, which we did in different ways, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that the result of the accused's political ambitions might have been the same in practical terms as those seeking a Greater Serbia? Yes, you do. Do you indeed make it clear that the accused might have about relying subtly or otherwise on the emotions that could be whipped up by those pressing for a philosophy that he wasn't prepared publicly to state? Yes, you do, because of course it may be that public expression of the Greater Serbia concept has negative potential within it. So that there may be several reasons for stating it, but we only ever stated it, certainly by the time that the matter had been argued in the Appeals Chamber to correct any misunderstanding at the Trial Chamber level and in my opening. We only ever expressed it in the cautious way that I've explained, but it would have been unhelpful to the Chamber because it was bound to arise, not at least to mention it, and mention it we did because it falls from the lips of others. Ambassador Galbraith. I couldn't rehearse Ambassador Galbraith in a proofing session and say, You think this is Greater Serbia. We've express it had differently, could I? I had to let him express himself as he would. I can't go to the military witnesses whose evidence was summarised in the passage Mr. Kay referred to and say, Well, that's the way you see it. We don't see it that way in a complex of history and philosophy and politics, and we want this phrase, not that. Of course not. Witnesses have to be allowed to express their view in the way that they did, and we are then left at the end with the position in which we are. And although I haven't got all the references for you, I can recall that in my questioning of the witnesses who dealt with the concept of Greater Serbia, I sought to make plain, and it's unfortunate if it didn't come across to the Chamber, but I sought to make plain that of course there was a difference between the expression of the concept of Greater Serbia with all its historical baggage or whatever you'd like to describe it and the actual objectives of this particular accused. And -- I don't think I can take it any further than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
