utterances.text: Do you say then -- do you say that Greater Serbia as you understand it is something different from all Serbs living within the same state?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Indeed. The plan -- because it has a different historical root. You've heard, for example, what this witness has said and I'm not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: His concept is quite clear and that it's not the same as what you're trying to portray here in the case against the accused. That's quite clear. But what I would like to understand is what you mean by a Greater Serbia. Do you mean that the concept as generally understood in the region is meant to -- or means all Serbs living within one state, or are you saying it's something different from that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Because you're using the expression repeatedly. If we go through your 98 bis response, if we go through the motion for joinder, the Prosecution are using the expression. They're putting it in inverted commas most of the time but not always. So they obviously have something in mind when they use it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's a centralised -- the centralised Serbian state incorporating those parts of both Croatia and Bosnia where Serbs lived or where Serbs could be located following, for example, the fall of the eastern enclaves and which could perhaps ultimately be attached to Serbia to form a single state, yes. But of course it's a different concept from that of this witness who has already recently given his expressed views on indeed the national of Croats, merely being Serbs by another name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But is there some other evidence or some or witness who says that Greater Serbia equals the concept you describe as all Serbs living within one state? Or is Greater Serbia as you refer to it in all these documents something different. That's what I'd like to understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Greater Serbia, the way that the Prosecution has used in inverted commas or applied with the phrase de facto and expressed in its questioning, that use of the Greater Serbia concept always distinct from the historical philosophical concept is the understanding of the objective of this accused and of those with whom he was in a joint criminal enterprise to have Serbs from Croatia and Bosnia centralised with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What evidence bears that out, Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That is what the case is about. Where we go to find it is in many different places. First of all, the facts on the ground, what people were doing. There's the express desires of various local groups that they might ultimately become identified with and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What part of the evidence. Yes, I know that evidence is there, but what part of the evidence explicitly relates that phenomenon to the Greater Serbia? That's what I wanted to find out. Because that is what you say you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, I'm reminded by Mr. Saxon, or maybe by Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, I'm not sure, that one witness, for example, General Adikic [phoen], actually made the equation in those terms. But it's -- this is a matter of fact, if I may say so, ultimately for the Chamber because labelling things is something we have to do for the processes of getting on with the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: With respect, Mr. Nice, you're not answering the question. In paragraph 262 of your response to the 98 bis motion, you say: "This amounted - de facto -"

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May I just find it for a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think I've got that -- is this the joinder one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. Your response the 98 bis motion, which is at a much later stage in the case and therefore more relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, I have it. Paragraph?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: 262. It says this: This amounted - de facto - to planning for a Greater Serbia."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, that means that Greater Serbia is a concept. It's a concept, and the evidence is that as a matter of fact what was happening was planning coincidentally which amounted to the same thing, but you have to have definition of the Greater Serbia to start with before you can say something de facto amounts to that. You've got to have the starting point. Now, what is the starting point?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it's no doubt my shortcoming, but I'm not sure that I do understand Your Honour's question. What we are saying here -- let me just go back to the previous paragraph. It says this: "The accused's plans," this is 261. "The accused's plan in the late 1980s, increasingly clear in 1990, was that the Serbian people scattered throughout the former Yugoslavia should live or remain in one state, the state in which they had a majority." And that's Jovic's diary cited. "The evidence shows that he was a head of Serb leaders in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina in planning and in the execution of the plan. In the case of Bosnia and Herzegovina, he conceived the plan together with Bosnian Serb leadership as early as 1991, perhaps before, that Serbs in Bosnia should remain part of one state linked territorially and politically to Serbia and to the Serb designated areas in Croatia." The footnote to that is various parts of evidence and intercepts which we'd have to look at in detail. So that what I'm saying, what we're saying there is that the evidence about his understanding and intention in the late 1980s and in the late 1990s to have, as we put it here, "Serbs in Bosnia should remain part of one state linked territorially and politically to Serbia and to Serb designated territories in Croatia amounted de facto to planning for a Greater Serbia."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no. That is a statement of the de facto position. That is the factual situation, and you then say that amounts to planning for a Greater Serbia. In other words, it comes to the same thing, you say, or -- but that you must have a starting -- Greater Serbia must mean something to start with.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see. Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And that's what I'm trying to find out. What is it you say that Greater Serbia is that the de facto actions of the accused amounted to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. It may be that this particular pleading would have been assisted by the -- by the single word "a" being either underlined or bolded because what we're -- in my reading of it it's quite clear, I think, it amounted to planning for a Greater Serbia. Now, if you take, as we have encouraged you to do from time to time, the Epoka maps which set out, for example, various versions of his party's ambitions at times proximate to The Hague Conference and matters of that sort, one can see that in a pragmatic way and an inevitably realistic way as politicians well or badly intentioned, the precise limits of their ambition will change from day to day and reflect changing circumstances, but they can all amount to plans to extend the Serbian state, so that what we are articulating here at this part of the filing is that there was a desire for a Greater Serbia, an enlarged Serbia, a centralised state of Serbs from Serbia and also from Croatia and Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And you would offer the same explanation for paragraph 252, which Judge Kwon read.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If I could have another look at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: "It is the Prosecution case that the accused intended to destroy the Muslim population of those parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina essentially earmarked for inclusion into a Greater Serbia."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. I think -- I seem to remember that the way I expressed it probably in opening - it may have been in one of the other arguments - it was to either gain or regain territory of this kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you further read that paragraph, the third sentence says like this: "The Bosnian Muslim population was the principal obstacle to its territorial designs, and he could not tolerate their existence as a group in those municipalities." So from that passage, am I correctly understanding that your -- the crux of the Prosecution case or the understanding of Greater Serbia is that it is related to the territorial design and not to tolerate the existence of other groups? So when the accused is saying that all Serbs should live in one state, he means this thing. His ambition related to territory and the expulsion of other ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So that's your understanding?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It includes that. You have two different -- you have two different developing problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Your understanding of Greater Serbia means same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Not the witness' Greater Serbia, the de facto Greater Serbia, yes, because there are two distinct parts, I suppose, depending how you want to split things up. There is ensuring that places where Serbs were in a majority could be in the same state. There is ensuring that places for other reasons it might have wanted to be Serb majority should fall into the same potential for inclusion, and that's the eastern Drina and Srebrenica for example in particular. So yes, there are -- but in a way Your Honour's question, picking up the factual difficulties facing the accused if he wanted a contiguous Serb state, show how inappropriate it might be simply to seek to fix him with a philosophical concept historically based rather than to say as we've said, and I would submit at all times, this was a practical plan of his. I've got another note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is it --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is it then your case that the proposed Greater Serbia was to in fact be one country incorporating Serbia and parts of Croatia and Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's always been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One country, one state.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Ultimately the intention thought would have been for these states to exist as a single state, and there is material coming from various sources that would show that that was the ambition of others however cautiously expressed or not expressed by this particular accused. But of course this particular accused, as he makes it plain, was prepared to play a long game and wait and see what developed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Which is different from preserving the state, a federal state, Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, yes. Once the possibility for preserving federal Yugoslavia was gone, whether at his own hands at The Hague Conference or otherwise, then a second plan has to come -- or doesn't have to come into effect, but it does come into effect, and that's the stage at which a Greater Serbia became the reality in his mind, we would argue. Let me just see if I've got anything else I want to draw your to attention. Yes. I mean, I don't -- I don't think we can understate nor have we understated the reality that the borders for which the accused's intentions and the actions to which he was associated would reach would have been similar to if not very similar or identical to in fact those espoused by this witness, thus the time that we've taken and I'm sorry that again the points haven't been made with sufficient clarity, the points we've -- the time we've taken with the historical maps, the London conference and so on, upon which the accused has relied or upon which his party has sought to rely. You will remember, for example, how it is that when he was seeking resolution of a problem he's caught on an intercept referring to somebody else's plan at the end of the First World War saying, Well, how about the London conference? Can't we go for that plan? This is the practical realities or the practical approach of this particular accused, but the extent would be the same as that espoused probably by this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But that -- well, is that your case, that the accused was going -- was seeking to take over the whole of Bosnia, for example? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, that's not the case that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, this witness says the whole of Bosnia falls within Greater Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, if you move it all up to the Karlobag-Virovitica line, yes, but the evidence we have at the moment is that the accused was at this stage much more pragmatic. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it's wrong to say that your case is that the intentions would reach or have been very similar to if not very similar or identical to in fact those espoused by this witness. They're quite different.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At this stage, correct. But, of course, if -- if you find that there is a cleaving to the Virovitica-Karlobag line ultimately is the plan with a much diminished Croatian state, then that's what comes about. We have to deal with things as they slowly unfolded. And with a man who, of course -- I'm not sure if this is protected or otherwise. No, I better not say that. I'm not sure. We're in public session. Just one minute. Would Your Honours just give me a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In any event -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm grateful that amongst other things for a reminder that again a couple of witnesses, and I think -- or one -- Matovina is one and Kandic is another, themselves specifically expressed, I haven't found the references, and I'm grateful to my friends for reminding me of them, but specifically refer to, as it were, a Greater Serbia putting the emphasis on "a" rather than on the concept. And that's -- these again are not witnesses we rehearse into their statement of their understanding nor could we, but they express what -- how they saw things. Now, I think it's also important to bear in mind with, as you view this part of the history of the case and as the issues that you're going to have to deal with that connection to the historical concept of Greater Serbia is not only something that may exist on a practical level, may exist on a practical level as between this accused and the concept itself, but for example it's something that might exist as a connection between the SANU memorandum and the concept of Greater Serbia, but all those understated or unstated. And therefore, it's far better to -- in our respectful submission far more -- and far more realistic to say what was this man seeking to achieve? He was seeking to achieve an enlarged centralised Serbian state. In many ways, picking up on His Honour Judge Bonomy's point, but not at the time always, it would have matched the ambitions of or part of the ambitions of people like this particular witness. It reflected other ideas, for example, the SANU memorandum without being stated by him. But what we're concerned with in this court is whether what he did by way of seeking to establish a Greater Serbian state involves the commission of the crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, would you care just to summarise what the Prosecution's case is on this point in just two or three sentences.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. This is -- I'm grateful to Mr. Saxon. The accused asked -- no, no. The accused -- the accused asked a question of a witness Erstic and the 25th of July, 2003, this question. He said: "Which speech of mine did you hear in which something was said that might have been against the Croats or against any people in Yugoslavia? Which speech did you hear? "Answer: Yes, sir. I watched you on television yourself when you were holding those rallies in Belgrade, when you were shouting, We want a Greater Serbia and all Serbs have to live in one state." Now, that's his recollection of the way things were expressed. I don't have it on a videotape, but there's a witness making a connection between his understanding of in whatever loose or technical form the term "Greater Serbia" and all Serbs living in one state. And we have been clear, I've been clear, that in answer to Your Honour Judge Robinson's point, the ambitions of this accused at the material time and once the possibility for retaining the former Federal Republic of Yugoslavia were gone, his ambitions were to have an enlarged or he was party to the ambitions to have an enlarged Serbian state and that informed his actions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: An enlarged Serbian state.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. De facto Greater Serbia, however you describe it. But not the concept of this man, this witness, or his party. At least as expressed. I see I have another note. Yes. I think I've made this point but if not I'm happy to either repeat myself or restate what I've already stated for greater clarity, that is that once the decision had been made to let Slovenia go, Croatia was allowed to go or it was contemplated that Croatia could go on terms that it left but without the parts that were going to remain under Serbian control, and at that stage, again to pick up on His Honour Judge Bonomy's point it wasn't the plan at that stage to include all of Bosnia except that. They faced the realities and restricted themselves to the parts as the accused himself says in various places dealing with it by percentages that it was realistic for them to retain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nice. This is essentially a matter for the Prosecutor, clarifying what his case is, so I'm not requiring submissions either from Mr. Kay or Mr. Milosevic, but if you have anything to say Mr. Kay, then you may say it, and similarly Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Milosevic, anything to say on this point bearing in mind, as I said, it's essentially for the Prosecutor to clarify what his case is.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is absolutely clear to me, Mr. Robinson, that you asked this question of him. However, since Mr. Nice stated many things that are not correct, I do have a need to speak, because he spoke for 40 minutes. First of all, Serbs in one state is no slogan. That was and had been a reality for a full 70 years, from the creation of Yugoslavia until 1991 what certain republics started to secede in an unlawful way and through armed conflicts. So Serbs in one state was a reality for 70 years. And if Mr. Nice accuses anyone of trying to preserve a state that was the only internationally recognised entity and a founding member of the United Nations from the First World War, then I suppose the list of those who can be accused of the same is really long. So let us leave that aside. Also, Mr. Robinson, you used an expression to the effect they should live in one state. That is wrong. They lived in one state. It was not a theory about how they should live in the future. They lived in one state and it was for the preservation of that state that we worked. Now, this is probably the first and the only instance in any trial, although you probably know more about trials, maybe you know of some other instance of this, that the Prosecution, after three and a half years since the beginning of their case, is not aware of what exactly their charges are. I think this Prosecution will be studied at universities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution don't know and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't think it's correct to say that they're not aware of what the charges are. The question has to do with the policy behind the Prosecution case, what the case actually is, not the actual charges.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, an even greater problem here is that at your insistence - and when I say "your insistence" I mean all three of you - if everything were clear, you probably wouldn't have any need to insist, but you do insist. It means it isn't clear, so at your insistence he's trying to clarify what exactly the case is. So what is the sense of all that he has been saying far? It is my fundamental right to know what I'm being accused of in order to answer these accusations. Another thing: In the past hour, Mr. Nice changed his position three times, one more nonsensical than the other. First, he said that he was not accusing me of advocating a Greater Serbia. It's all in the transcript. I don't need to quote it. Let us not manipulate what has been said here. Then he does accuse me of it, and then is that the same thing as all Serbs in one state with Yugoslavia having existed as a state for 70 years, and then he goes on to manipulate facts. He just mentioned the testimony of Academician Popov and some part of map, whereas it has been shown quite clearly that Mr. Nice manipulated those Epoka maps. It was a magazine that was published in Belgrade. Karlobag-Ogulin-Virovitica line was in a map that was published in this magazine, and then some sort of link is being made with me, but he doesn't mention that there was a text next to the map where it says that those are writing it do not agree with the map. So it's pure manipulation. The map of the Belgrade initiative according to which Izetbegovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The word "manipulation" has come across in the translation. It's -- you're on safer ground if you say that he misinterpreted the map. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He did not misinterpret it. He showed a map accompanied by a text which expresses a critical attitude to the map that the magazine was advocating. It is clear that this was done deliberately, and it is pure lie. The Belgrade initiative map that Izetbegovic was pushing, when he was president of that state, he showed as the map of Greater Serbia. He's consciously deceiving everyone here. You probably missed it. He just said about the possibility for the SFRY to survive, he just said he, meaning I, did it at The Hague Conference. The Hague Conference offered a break-up of Yugoslavia that I refused. So it's quite the opposite. He simply doesn't know what he's talking about anymore. Either that or he's presenting notorious lies that are so obvious that I don't know what to say. I've already told you that Mr. Nice should be held criminally responsible for deliberate obstruction of truth and deceit, because he has had all the facts --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic. Mr. Milosevic, you're getting carried away. I said initially that this was primarily a matter for the Prosecutor to clarify what his case is. He has done that. If you have any submissions to make on that particular legal issue, legal issue, then you may make them. I am allowing you to speak, even though I don't consider it to be absolutely necessary, because I want to be fair to you, because it impinges on your case, but you must confine your submissions to legal issues. Don't make accusations.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Robinson, it is also a legal issue. Even now when he is trying to explain at your request, and you didn't make that request because everything was clear to you but because it isn't clear to you. He's now talking about A and B plans. Where does he take that from? Did he present any evidence here about plans A and B? Then he mentioned an intercept where Milosevic is allegedly heard saying, And where is the London conference map? The London conference map was mentioned by my collocutor in that intercept, whereas I was extremely uninterested. That is the sort of manipulation that I believe no one should allow. And look, Mr. Nice is supposed to time his references to Greater Serbia. He says this is when I mentioned it the first time, and this is when I mentioned it the last time. He was supposed to establish a basis, although Mr. Kay already warned him that no human being can stand a trial longer than two and a half years, and still you went through with it. Then he says he doesn't link the plan with me and I didn't say that. Then on page 82 in his opening, the army, the evidence was no better -- "the evidence shows it was no better." "[In English] Committed itself to the accused's programme." [Interpretation] Is there any clearer than that. "Officers were being instilled with the ideology of brotherhood and unity, totally abandoned everything in favour of Greater Serbia." This is very explicit. I therefore insist, gentlemen, that we clear up first of all what I'm being charged with and then I can make my case. Then if you will look at the testimony of academician Cedomir Popov. It's page 34587. Mr. Nice says: "Can I also by way -- not by way of correction but reminder alert the Chamber and the accused to the reality that neither in my opening speeches to this Court in my own name or behalf of the Prosecution rely upon the words 'Greater Serbia.'" Just look at that. During the testimony of Popov, he distanced himself from it, whereas now he relies on his opening. I used the phrase once. [In English] With the man Seselj [Interpretation] associating it with the man Seselj. That is not true. He referred to Greater Serbia mentioning man Seselj but not in his opening statement. In his opening statement it was associated with me, whereas now he says that the Prosecution never relied on Greater Serbia. "[In English] I used the phrase once associating with the man Seselj, and I think on two occasions I referred to the concept of all Serbs in one state." [Interpretation] Again, he doesn't know what he's talking about. All Serbs in one state, that was the Yugoslavia we were trying to preserve. And the phrase the "Greater Serbia" which has never been attributed to the mouth of the accused is the concept that has been referred to by many other witnesses, and of course we can't control them in their and analysis and understanding. Well, is Mr. Nice now going to withdraw those witnesses that he cannot control and who misunderstood him? Now he says that we heard testimony from some witness who heard me on television asking for Greater Serbia. All my speeches were recorded by television. They were attended by thousands and millions of people. These are blatant lies. Blatant lies. According to the practice supplied here, he can lead evidence here and make claims that everybody knows is a notorious lie. This is just the tip of the iceberg of this fiasco that we Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. are facing here. Then Judge Robinson, before that he says: "[In English] [Previous translation continues] ... is a concept that's been referred to by many other witnesses and of course we can't control them in their analysis and understanding of events. So far as the Prosecution is concerned, it's always been careful to limit its approach to the issue to the way I opened the case." [Interpretation] And I already quoted to you how he opened the Prosecution case. It was completely indecent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON ASKS THE QUESTION
utterances.text: "It is not in the indictment."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "[In English] It's in one of the indictments as well but those of course preceded my openings, and my opening in the sense of the matter of general theory and principle surprised them but you are quite right."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: "But you're not saying it's not an important part of the Prosecution case." Mr. Nice: "I'm not saying that. Not at all. No. It's an important, it's an important matter to have in mind but we always expressed ourselves in term of all Serbs in one state." [Interpretation] I've just read to you what he said. "We've always expressed a notion in one way or another instrumentalising the opinion of others." I believe that you should demand from Mr. Nice, Mr. Robinson, to define precisely what his case is and stop this until he does. He just mentioned what people did in Bosnia, in Croatia. People were defending themselves. It was not Serbs who started armed secession and civil war. All the evidence you have before you indicate that for months prior to that others had started killing them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I did ask Mr. Nice to summarise the Prosecution's case on this point, and in answer he said that the concept that the Prosecution embraces is that of an enlarged Serbian state. So that's the position now. We have all the evidence before us. We have the transcript that we can look at. I want to proceed with the case now. I consider that matters --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you tell me, because you have been presiding for a while and you have been here from the start, which evidence did he present that I worked for an enlarged Serbian state? Was there any evidence that he presented on that account?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, that is beside the point. That is his case. I mean, if we find that it is not substantiated, then that will be reflected in the determinations that we make. So we don't have to make a determination of that issue now, as you well know. It is important that you know what you are facing, and he has clarified it. So let us proceed. Ask your next question of this witness. And I'd like to move on to another issue, another subject area.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, precisely in order to clarify this, I think the witness who said this himself, and he wouldn't be lying about that, is a leading theoretician on the issue. I accept Mr. Nice's comment that he's not testifying as an expert here, but he wrote a book about this, and the subject can be found in many other books of his. He is currently a politician, the head of the largest opposition party. He's a very qualified witness, so he can speak about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you're going to ask him about the concept of an enlarged Serbian state?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why? Why not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Yes, I'll allow that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Seselj, I wish to ask you, you've already answered the question of the Croatian response to the concept you are advocating, but tell me this: Do the vehicles, the protagonists of this concept, advocate or did they ever advocate the destruction of Muslims?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The Serbian Radical Party made a geographical map of the larger -- sorry, Greater Serbia, and from that map which we published countless times on the cover page of the colour back side of our magazine, one can say that the western border of the Greater Serbia is on the Karlobag-Ogulin-Virovitica line. That does not contain only territories where Serbs are in the majority. It contains also many territories where Croats, Macedonians, and Muslims are majority population. If somebody says that our intention was to expel all those people, that's nonsense because it would be an exodus. Second, at the time when the Yugoslav crisis was peaking, I wrote a letter to the Serbs of the Muslim faith. It was an open letter published several times where I say, "Muslim brothers, do not let yourselves be deceived as you were deceived in the two world wars, to be the tool in the hands of the enemies of your Serbian brothers." That was published in books, in the press. This can be put at your disposal. We wish --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Seselj. Mr. Milosevic, bear in mind that the Prosecution's case relates to the idea of an enlarged Serbian state.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am bearing it in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, was there ever any mention of Serbia having any territorial pretensions?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No one ever expressed a position about territorial pretensions on the part of Serbia. Serbs in the federal territorial unit clearly said to the Croats, "If you want to secede from Yugoslavia, we don't want to. We will remain in Yugoslavia. That is why we are setting up the Serbia Krajina." The Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina clearly gave the Croats and Muslims to understand that if they wished to secede from Yugoslavia, the Serbs did not and wished to remain in Yugoslavia. This was stated clearly at the beginning of every war. "We do not want to leave Yugoslavia, but you do." Nobody avoided talks about how one could leave Yugoslavia. Cutileiro's plan was even drawn up in Bosnia, accepted by the Muslims and, Serbs but under American pressure the Muslims later changed their mind. What the Orthodox Serbs wanted was the preservation of Yugoslavia, not an enlarged Serbia. Most of Serbs didn't even want a Greater Serbia. It was only the Serb Radical Party that wanted it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That point has been made, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, a little while ago Mr. Nice explained his position. He quoted something, probably from one of his documents, saying that it was my plan to expel Muslims from part of the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I assume the Serb-controlled parts. He, of course, did not support this with any evidence, but that's what he claims. Could you explain, please, how it is possible for someone to have a plan to expel Muslims from Serb-controlled parts of Bosnia while not expelling any Muslims from Serbia which is all under Serb control and where there is no war at all?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You cannot put a question in that form. I'll not allow that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, was there on my part or on the part of anyone in the Serb leadership that you know of a plan to expel Muslims from any part of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Never did there exist a plan on the expulsion of Muslims. You wanted Bosnia and Herzegovina to remain within Yugoslavia as a whole, even if Slovenia and Croatia secede, and you negotiated with Izetbegovic. As far as I know and remember, you offered Izetbegovic the position of the first president of the Rump Yugoslavia if a complete break-up could be avoided. Izetbegovic first accepted this and then changed his mind under American pressure. The Americans said to him, "Why would you want a Rump Yugoslavia when you can have full independence?" If all Serbs remained in one state, then all Muslims would also remain in one state, because the Muslims lived in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Serbia, and Kosovo and Metohija, Montenegro, and Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Seselj. Next question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, please look at paragraph 7 of the Croatian part and then 22.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment. Let me get my copy of the indictment as I have been a passive observer for more than an hour. You're saying paragraph 7?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Page 3 of the Croatian part.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It says here: "This joint criminal enterprise came into existence before the 1st of August, 1991, and continued until at least June 1992." So it says here sometime before the 1st of August, 1991. Now look at 22. It says here: "Vojislav Seselj, as president of the Serbian Radical Party, SRS, from at least February 1991 throughout the time relevant," so far about six months you were a participant in a joint criminal enterprise before it even came into existence. Can you please describe these crimes of yours so that we can hear what kind of crimes they are?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is truly totally absurd that I was a member of a joint criminal enterprise which came into existence sometime before the 1st of August, 1991, and yet I was its participant from at least February 1991. Well, perhaps I became participant when I was a baby. I have no answer to give to this. First of all, there was no joint criminal enterprise. Secondly, as for my participation in the war effort, I have already described it. I described it yesterday. Secondly, my advocation of a Greater Serbia has practically nothing to do with the civil war that was waged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very specific, very direct: Was there a joint criminal enterprise of which you could or could not be a member?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no joint criminal enterprise. I have never even met many of the people on this list.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, the question arises here as to how negative facts can be proved. Do you expect me to prove that what Mr. Nice alleges did not happen, that what Mr. Nice alleges did not exist or is it up to Mr. Nice to prove that it did exist?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: As you well know, the burden of proof is on the Prosecution. You don't have to prove a thing. You can sit there and remain silent and walk through that door at the end of the case a free man. You don't have to prove anything. Next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, before we move on to the next topic, look at the Bosnian part. Please look at paragraphs 7 and 22 of the Bosnian part. It says here -- in fact, it doesn't even have the words "at least." It says: "This joint criminal enterprise was in existence by the 1st of August, 1991, and continued until at least the 31st of December, 1995." So this covers Dayton and the end of Dayton. All of it was a joint criminal enterprise from the 1st of August. And now look at paragraph 22, which mentions you, and here it says again "at least," there was a joint criminal enterprise, according to paragraph 7, from the 1st of August, and you were its participant from at least February 1991.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the end of 1995 as alleged in paragraph 7. However, in the indictment raised against me it says I was a member of the JC until 1993. And the Prosecutor is the same in both cases, and they're both sitting here now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, do you have any idea why the 1st of August, 1991, is mentioned here as the date when this alleged JC came into existence?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because that was when the JNA came into conflict with the Croatian separatists and their paramilitary units. Approximately at that time the army started to respond to the armed action which it had been exposed to even before, but it had been too passive and refrained from returning fire. As far as I personally am concerned, from around the 1st of August onwards, we began sending volunteers to the JNA, but what I did from February 1991 until August 1991, I don't know what they think I was doing at the time, but what can it have to do with the rest of you mentioned here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, that has been answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, the question you raised at the end of your reply is something I really cannot answer, but we shall see.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I will be thinking about it for the next three years while I'm waiting for my trial to begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let me see now. Paragraph -- well, you have to read paragraph 9 in both parts, the Croatian and the Bosnian parts, because it says here "In order for the joint criminal enterprise to succeed in its objective, Slobodan Milosevic worked in concert with or through other individuals in the joint criminal enterprise. Each participant or co-perpetrator within the joint criminal enterprise sharing the intent to contribute to the enterprise played his or her own role or roles that significantly contributed to achieving the objective of the enterprise. The roles of the participants or co-perpetrators include but are not limited to the following," and then you are mentioned. Is it clearer to you now what crimes you're accused of, Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, of course not. But, Mr. Milosevic, how can they link me up to you when the two of us met for the first time in our lives in April 1992, and we had allegedly been members of this joint criminal enterprise for a year?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, when we met, when and where was this, and did we talk about something?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was in the building of the national assembly. You came to the session. You were sitting in the front row. I came along, and we only shook hands as a matter of courtesy. Afterwards we met in the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. corridor and walked down the stairs together, and we had a very casual conversation about the session of that day. That was our first meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This was 1992?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: April 1992. I am sure of that. The press recorded that meeting. Our photograph together was published in many newspapers. We had never met before that occasion or had any contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And if you remember, when did we first meet to discuss a political topic? When was our first meeting to talk?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in May 1992, when at your invitation I came to the Presidency of Serbia and we discussed the forthcoming federal elections. You wanted to hear whether the Serbian Radical Party would participate in the elections because all the other opposition parties under American influence had stated they would boycott the first federal elections after the adoption of the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain why these opposition parties, some opposition parties, I can't say all of them because you were one of the largest at the time and you did not boycott the elections, why did they boycott the first federal elections for the parliament of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Following orders from the American embassy because the Americans were avoiding having to recognise the continuity, the legal continuity, although it -- of the state, although it was recognised by the People's Republic of China and other countries. The People's Republic of China was the first state to recognise the continuity of the state. The US instrumentalised the opposition parties. They wanted them to not participate in the elections in order to challenge the continuity of the state and in order to use them as a tool against our country.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And these federal parliamentary elections, were they held in spite of this? Were they successful, and did citizens turn out in a higher percentage that than they do now?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The turnout was much higher than now. The elections were very successful, and it transpired that the Serb Radical Party was the second most powerful political party in the country, of course thanks to the boycott by all the other opposition parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a quarter past 12.00. Is it time for a break, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you for reminding me, Mr. Milosevic. We will adjourn now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, before I go on, please consider my motion. I move that this excerpt from Mr. Seselj's book, "The Ideology of Serb Nationalism," be exhibited. It has been translated and delivered to you and all participants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it's admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now let us clarify something, Mr. Seselj. But before we do, I have to put a question to Mr. Robinson. For you, Mr. Seselj, in paragraph 7 of the Bosnian paper, it says that this joint criminal enterprise was in existence by the 1st of August. In paragraph 9, it says that each participant implemented a part of the plan, and then in paragraph 22 you are mentioned as part of this joint criminal enterprise from February 1991 at least. For the witness and myself to be clear about what this is about, Mr. Robinson, please have Mr. Nice explain, because it's a consistent text and he wrote both parts, whether this alleged JCE of which I was at the head and which Mr. Seselj participated in came into existence on the 1st of August as is stated if paragraph 7 or from at least February 1991 as mentioned in paragraph 22, because the discrepancy is six months, and this is very important. Could Mr. Nice please tell us from when he believes there was a joint criminal enterprise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That is not the kind of matter that I'd ask the Prosecutor to explain. If you believe that there is a discrepancy, then it can only add on to your benefit, and that's a point you would make in your closing remarks.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, what I believe or not doesn't matter at this point, but the difference between the 1st of August and February is a discrepancy of six months. I don't know what kind of criminal enterprise Mr. Nice is referring to, one that began on the 1st of August or one that began in February. So how can I put questions to Mr. Seselj about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's clear to me, Mr. Milosevic, from the 1st of February I myself was a member of the JCE. I joined myself, and then six months later you and the others joined me. I understood this immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Seselj. You have greatly assisted Mr. Nice, and I'm glad you are cooperating with him so well. I will continue with my questions now. Mr. Seselj, in paragraph 7 of the Croatian part, the following members of the JCE are listed. It says here: "Individuals participating in this joint criminal enterprise included," it begins with me, of course, and then it goes on to list a number of people. The next is Borislav Jovic. What was your relationship with Borisav Jovic?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never had any contacts or meetings with Borislav Jovic. I had never had any until that session that you attended and Borislav Jovic also attended it. In 1991, at the elections in Rakovica when there was a seat in parliament up for election, I was there representing my party and Borislav Jovic was representing a rival party. I will remind you he was at that time the president of the Socialist Party, and he was holding a counter-rally to support the candidate of your party.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's not unusual.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But we were members of opposing political parties, rival parties, and we had never met. I defeated your party's candidate resoundingly. I had three times more votes than he did but I won't bring that up now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, you have answered my question very precisely. So you did not have anything to do with Borislav Jovic.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The next one on the list is Branko Kostic, who at the time, as far as I can recall, was the deputy president of the Presidency of the SFRY, and he was elected in the Republic of Montenegro, which he represented in the Presidency of the SFRY. What were your relations with Branko Kostic?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time in my life I spoke to Branko Kostic was at the federal elections in late May 1992 when the Federal Assembly was constituted in June and when a candidate for the Presidency was Svetozar Markovic. Our party opposed this, and we said that we would nominate Branko Kostic as our candidate. We didn't really know him but they were both from Montenegro, and we thought it better for Kostic to be nominated. Then, Mr. Milosevic, you invited me for a talk, and you suggested that we nominate Dobrica Cosic. I agreed and that's how we gave up nominating Branko Kostic. But I didn't know the man at all. He was reputed to be a very honourable man, but you convinced me that Dobrica Cosic was a better candidate at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As the next in this JCE is Veljko Kadijevic. What was your relation to Veljko Kadijevic?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had never met Veljko Kadijevic in my life. We never talked about anything. We had no contact whatsoever. However, I often attacked him in public. I considered him to be a rigid communist, a dogmatic communist at first, and afterwards I had my doubts. I thought that he was an American spy. He completed a school for generals in the United States, and his behaviour during the war was suspicious so I often attacked him, and I thought that he should be replaced.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did I understand you properly? You said that you never met him in your life?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never met him in my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you did not even talk over the telephone? You never met him?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we never talked even over the telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what about the next person in this joint criminal enterprise that Mr. Nice has been insisting upon here, Blagoje Adzic.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I first met him after the promulgation of the constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia towards the end of April 1992 at the grand reception after the parliament meeting was held. This was just before he was pensioned off. This was just a courtesy handshake. Perhaps we exchanged a word or two. We never discussed anything of substance. I had nothing to talk about to him, although in public I expressed a negative view of him, perhaps like of Kadijevic, but in a somewhat milder form.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The next person in this paragraph 7 is Milan Babic. Tell me, please, what was your attitude towards Milan Babic at the time as an alleged participant in this joint criminal enterprise?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met Milan Babic at the end of August or beginning of September 1990. We had proper relations. We did not see each other often. We did not contact very often, but I think that our relations were relatively good until the first democratic multi-party elections for the national assembly of the Republic of Serb Krajina. That was towards the end of 1993. At these elections, the Serb Radical Party won a very large number of seats in parliament. Babic's party was individually the biggest party in parliament. We agreed that our parties would set up a coalition and a coalition government that he would head. He cheated us after that. He reached an agreement with Borislav Mikelic and joined Mikelic's government as Foreign Minister. Since then I've never seen him again, and I never spoke of him well since because I thought this was a person who did not deserve any kind of political communication because I thought that this was a vile thing to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's just dwell on Milan Babic for a second. Do you remember that I had a clash with him or, rather, that I criticised his behaviour on some occasion? I don't want to put a leading question to you so I'm not going to tell you what occasion that was. But at any rate, very publicly there was a dispute. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was on the occasion of the Vance Plan. This was sometime in January 1992, if my memory serves me right. The talks were held in Belgrade at the initiative expressed by the West that the leadership of Serbia and the SFRY should take part in concluding the Vance Plan. Milan Babic was a hard-liner at the time. I don't know whether you personally attended this big meeting of the state Presidency and the state leadership in general. He was talked into accepting the plan. I think that the president of the national assembly Mile Paspalj signed that agreement. Since Milan Babic speaks until -- sleeps until 2.00 or 3.00 in the afternoon, that was taken advantage of. This meeting was scheduled for 9.00 a.m., and that is how it went through.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This meeting that you referred to was held at the Presidency of the SFRY. I was not a member, but you put it right that it was --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said that you were present. I said that you publicly supported the Vance Plan. I did not say that you were one of the participants in the meeting. Actually, I had no way of knowing because I was not personally present. It is my knowledge that this meeting was held. It was published in the media that this meeting was held, and it is my knowledge that he was the only one who opposed accepting the Vance Plan and that everybody else was in favour of it. I never said that you were present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I understand what you were saying, but I want that to be expressed clearly here for the sake of the transcript. It was a bit unclear. And in this dispute between me and Babic, on whose side were you?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the dispute between you and Milan Babic, I was on the side of Milan Babic, although after some talks with a group of prominent intellectuals in Belgrade, I subsequently supported the Vance Plan. Unfortunately, later on that proved to be a mistake because we were cheated both by the Western powers and the United Nations. However, at that moment, I was on Milan Babic's side. I wanted in a way for political relations to be improved between Serbia and the SFRY and the authorities of the Serb Krajina. I thought that there shouldn't be any clashes there, especially not in public because that could work to the detriment of overall state and national interests.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You actually explain now why you supported Babic in these disputes.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is that the only thing you can say about the reasons why you did that?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I personally preferred his hard-line policy towards the Croatian leadership and the Western powers rather than your policy of reconciliation and agreement. You always wanted agreement. You always wanted compromise. You were in favour of dialogue, and I regularly had a much more hard-line position. I always preferred people who, like me, took these hard-line positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 7, the next person who is mentioned as a participant in this alleged joint criminal enterprise is Milan Martic. What was your attitude towards Milan Martic as a participant in this alleged joint criminal enterprise?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met Milan Martic and saw him whenever I came to the Serb Krajina. At first our relations were good and then we clashed in 1993 when there was a fierce clash between the Serb Radical Party and your Socialist Party of Serbia. It was then that Milan Martic issued some kind of a press release against the Serb Radical Party, and that's when the period of our conflict started. In the elections of the Serb Krajina held that autumn, the Serb Radical Party had Rade Leskovac, the then president of the Serb Radical Party for the Republic of Serb Krajina, as its own presidential Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. candidate. We did not support either Babic or Milan Martic. But in the second round, when it was Milan Babic and Milan Martic who got into the second round, we fully supported Milan Babic. Almost all other political parties supported Milan Martic. As far as I can remember, your Socialist Party held the view that Martic was a better solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you think today that Milan Martic was a better solution that Milan Babic?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Time proved Milan Martic to be an exceptionally honest and honourable man, in spite of our dispute, somebody who never violated any kind of morality. As for Babic, he turned out to be a really rotten person, and I am really sorry that I favoured the other person at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of what did you come to that conclusion that he was such a bad person, such a rotten person, as you said?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of many things. First of all, his attitude towards the coalition that we set up, and then also that he heard that there would be a Croat aggression against the republic of Serb Krajina in 1995. He tacitly sent his family to Belgrade and his compatriots remained and were victimised in other parts then -- of Krajina. Then also he appeared as a false witness in many of these proceedings. He was also heralded or rather announced as a false witness in my trial. I am not disclosing any secrets because it was said in public.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker please be asked to slow down, note the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: A request from the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, in paragraph 7, the next person referred to as an alleged participant in the alleged joint criminal enterprise is Goran Hadzic. What can you say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There's a terminological choice of this witness. I expect the Chamber's alert to it, but where he says that Mr. Babic was heralded or announced as a witness in the trial, he's correct, but the way he prefaces the word witness with "false" might in some way lead the reader to think that there was some acknowledgement in those prosecuting this particular witness that the -- that Babic was not being relied upon. Babic is being relied upon. The word "false" is simply his characterisation of the person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Nice. That would be noted. It's the witness's own description. Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Please continue, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, will you allow me to say something? I followed the testimony of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, not on that at all. Absolutely no. Continue, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you believe or do you believe that Milan Babic is someone oriented only towards his career, someone who is a liar and someone who always tries to gets benefits for himself only?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. I followed him on television too and --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... and I say no more about it. That's clearly an objectionable form of question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I will not allow that question. You'd have to rephrase it. It's leading, and it's -- it's objectionable. It's objectionable.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj. Mr. Seselj, Mr. Milan Babic is on the list of participants in the alleged joint criminal enterprise, the same list on which you are. Do you have any reasons or any facts to proffer as to why it bothers you to be in the same company as Milan Babic?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, no person from this list was in good relations with Milan Babic, and no one ever had a good opinion of him. I'm the only one that in a given period of time had sort of good relations with him. Milan Babic was a coward during the war. He never dared tour the troops at the front line. He was very narrow-minded, merchantile, and after the war he proved to be a bad person too. Over here Milan Babic said things that were untruthful. For example, he said that Marko Negovanovic, as minister of defence of Serbia, gave a helicopter that took me to Western Slavonia. And Marko Negovanovic at that time was not minister of defence of Serbia. It was Tomislav Simovic, who we also have on this list. That is one illustration for you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, yes. I think you have answered that question. Next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Seselj. I put a question to you in relation to Goran Hadzic. However, in view of Mr. Nice's intervention, you didn't have time to answer it so I'm repeating the question. Not to add everything that I asked you in this connection, tell me about Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in constant conflict with Goran Hadzic, so our relationship was a hostile one. I attacked him strongly in the Sava centre at the pan-Serbian Assembly that was called that was intended to pass a decision to make the leadership of Republika Srpska adopt the Vance Plan. I attacked Goran Hadzic. You were at that session, so I perhaps -- perhaps you will remember that I attacked him ferociously, accusing him of crime and many other things. So we were never -- never on good terms, political or otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The next person is Jovica Stanisic on this list in terms of the joint criminal enterprise. Did you have any kind of relations with Jovica Stanisic in terms of what you have been accused of or what I have been accused of?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I first met Jovica Stanisic in November 1992 at his own initiative. He sent a message through some republican MP that we should meet. I agreed, and we met in front of the building of the national assembly. He came in some special luxury car with dark glass, armoured, and he warned me that an assassination was being prepared against me in Montenegro by a well-known Montenegrin criminal and head of the Montenegrin underground, Brano Micunovic. That was just before the new elections, the federal elections in 1992. The same information was given to me then by the head of the military security service then, Nedeljko Boskovic but he called me over the phone and told me that quite openly. Jovica Stanisic did not phone me. We didn't even know each other. He asked for a direct meeting, and he told me that. I did not even take part in this election campaign. I did not travel there at all. I had a bad back at the time. I had surgery, so in Montenegro I did not even carry out an election campaign.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please be asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj. Mr. Seselj, I knew the interpreters were going to intervene again because of the speed with which you speak. You get caught up with your own words, and you're carried away. You speak too fast.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I understand your problems and the problems of the interpreters, but you should bear in mind that the way in which I speak shows that I am speaking as a person who speaks the truth with passion. A person can speak this way only if he tells the truth, not if he lies. I hope that you will agree with me, but I will make an effort to speak slower.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Chamber will determine that. We are assessing your demeanour. Let me assure you of that. Now --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After that, I was constantly clashing with Jovica Stanisic. He was head of the State Security Service of Serbia, and after our fierce conflict with that service they made every effort to break up the Serb Radical Party. You probably remember the affair of trying to buy off seven of our MPs headed by Jovan Glamocanin [phoen] when they were given money to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker please be asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, you have to do better. And, Mr. Milosevic, it is not my responsibility alone. He is your witness. I have a job to control the proceedings, but he's your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, I've already thanked you for the information you've given in terms of knowing Jovica Stanisic and this substantive information you gave about his warning that an assassination was being prepared in Montenegro, that they were trying to kill you in Montenegro. The next person on the list is Franko Simatovic?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please pause after every sentence so that what the interpreters are interpreting would correctly be recorded by the transcript. So in relation to Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Franko Simatovic nicknamed Frenki is a person I had never seen in my life until Simatovic came to the prison of The Hague Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Seselj. Since you've said that, there is no further need for you to explain your relationship with him. You never met him in your life until he came here to The Hague Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is the full truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was your relationship with Tomislav Simovic who was minister of defence of Serbia for a while?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: While he was minister of defence of Serbia, I was an MP in the Assembly of Serbia. We saw each other from time to time at Assembly sessions. Our relationship was correct without being close. We never had any particular meetings or talks. When I was planning my trip to Western Slavonia at the proposal of Ilija Sasic, minister of defence of Western Slavonia, I addressed General Tomislav Simovic as minister of defence asking him to provide me with a helicopter. He replied that the Ministry of Defence of Serbia has no helicopter or any similar means of transportation. After that I addressed the deputy chief of General Staff, General Marko Negovanovic, who directed me to the commander of air force and air defence, Bozidar Stevanovic. So that was my only direct contact with Tomislav Simovic, and it was for only a particular purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you were an MP in the Assembly of Serbia at the time. Do you know what were the powers and the job of the Ministry of Defence of Serbia at the time? Did it have any armed forces?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tomislav Simovic, as minister of defence of Serbia, did not have any powers regarding the JNA. All his competencies related to civilian defence structure, and he may have had powers only to assist but not to command and control the Territorial Defence, because the Territorial Defence Staff had its own commander. So his powers were mainly to prepare civilian structures for possible defence of the country. He could have had certain powers regarding military departments and the inclusion of military conscripts in military service, regular military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Explain briefly what military departments are.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are regional. They're usually municipal departments of the Ministry of Defence that issue call-ups of military conscripts and sometimes the reserve force inviting them to take part in drills. Those are their main competencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When they invite reservists to military exercises, they are practically doing a job for the JNA?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because it is the JNA that organises military exercises, and the military departments only take it upon themselves to issue the call-ups.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So these are jobs linked to the TO?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That only was introduced in the 1970s and 1980s. They, too - I mean the Territorial Defence - were territorial bodies, because when a government was being formed the Prime Minister designate could not himself decide who the minister of defence would be. He had to ask the JNA for its opinion. He had to ask the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct. The next name on the list is your name. I will skip it. Followed by Momir Bulatovic. Tell me, what is your attitude toward Momir Bulatovic, especially as an alleged member, and please always bear that in mind, in the alleged JCE?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was president of the Republic of Montenegro. I first talked to him when an assassination attempt was made at me after a rally held in Podgorica, the capital of Montenegro. The assassin threw a hand-grenade that injured 62 participants in the rally including me. He was caught soon afterwards, and since I was in Montenegro with my wife, Momir Bulatovic, as president of the republic, came to the airport to see us off to Belgrade and to express his regret over the assassination attempt. After that I didn't have any particular meetings or talks with him for the entire duration of this period covered by the indictment. Of course later we had several meetings and encounters when he became Prime Minister of the federal government, which happened in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but it covers the period of Kosovo. And at one point your deputy Tomislav Nikolic was deputy Prime Minister in the federal government.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true. I meant the Croatian indictment. Yes, my deputy in the Radical Party was the deputy Prime Minister in the cabinet headed by Momir Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What is the relationship between your party, including Tomislav Nikolic, and yourself and Momir Bulatovic?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were various stages. Sometimes we were in conflict. Sometimes there were periods of cooperation. Generally I believe Momir Bulatovic is a rather honourable man, so I have no objection to him that way. But to say that we were any -- in any sort of joint enterprise would be too much, especially a criminal enterprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The next name in paragraph 7 is Aleksandar Vasiljevic. You mentioned yesterday the activities of Aleksandar Vasiljevic. Would you have anything to add to what you said yesterday? And I want to ask you in particular, in your relationship with Aleksandar Vasiljevic, because you're all covered by this general -- sorry, joint criminal enterprise, what was your relationship with him? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were always in conflict from the time when he was chief of security of the Sarajevo military district, when he prevented me to serve my military service in the school of military officers, something that was my great desire, but he stood in my way as chief of security of the Sarajevo military district. Then he moved to the General Staff in Belgrade as chief of the military security service, and as my political opponent, he spread rumours that I was raped while in prison in Zenica. That was a pure lie, but it was tendentiously spread, because at that time I was intolerable for the regime as a political opponent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Wait a minute. He wanted to humiliate you?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to humiliate me and also to disqualify me in the public. Because in our people, in our community, that is the greatest humiliation imaginable.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But when you say "regime," which regime do you mean?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean the former SFRY. That lie was launched into the Belgrade public in the end 1980s.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I wanted it to be clear on the record when the use -- when use is made of the word "regime," they usually mean the period when I was president.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I mean the other regime of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and I was talking about the JNA and the Ministry of Defence. Later on, I attacked Aleksandar Vasiljevic several times for his various activities in his capacity as chief of military security, and for a while he was in prison for that. If you remember the Opara and Labrada operations, the laying of explosives to the Jewish municipality and Jewish cemetery, and I accused him of stealing from the Vukovar bank during the liberation of Vukovar. He stole several million Deutschmark that he never turned over to the central bank. If that was war booty, that should have been, according to regulations, turned over to the central service. That money simply disappeared and I publicly accused Aleksandar Vasiljevic for that. I also accused him as chief of the military security of initiating certain crimes on the Serbian side in order to ascribe them to Serbian nationalists. I mean, crimes in Western Slavonia and crimes committed after the liberation of Vukovar. It is curious that he was always present on the ground when these things happened and nobody's prosecuting him for anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
