utterances.text: The next personality mentioned in paragraph 7 together with you in this alleged joint criminal enterprise is Radovan Stojicic, also known as Badza.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I first met Radovan Stojicic, called Badza, sometime in the summer 1991 in Erdut where he was staying as a volunteer of the Territorial Defence of Western Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem. I also met him at a celebration after the liberation of a part of Serbian Krajina. I think it was a year later. As assistant military police of Serbian commander or rather head of public security, a police general, he organised my arrest and the arrest of my closest associates from the Serbian Radical Party when we attempted to hold a rally in Gnjilane in the area of Kosovo and Metohija. On that occasion my deputy Tomislav Nikolic and I were convicted for misdemeanors, sentenced to two months in prison. Others got slightly lower sentences. Badza was killed in the first half of 1997 in a restaurant called Mama Mia in the centre of Belgrade. We have already spoken about the circumstances of his death during my previous testimony, but I can repeat if you insist. So we had no friendly relationship, no close relationship. We did meet, but he had always been in the fiercest conflict with us, with the radicals, as chief of police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When I questioned you about the claims of Mr. Nice, namely that Serbia was a police state between 1997 and 2000, and that it was not uncommon for some prominent people to be killed, that was mentioned. Radovan Stojicic Badza was a close associate of mine.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And he was a very renowned, well-reputed man, and the person who killed him certainly bore that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nice insisted also on some murders carried out by the police state. However, it was mainly my associates who were killed in these assassinations.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember Zoran Todorovic, my chef -- my -- the head of the Yugoslav left?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that. I publicly expressed my suspicion that it was Nenad Djordjevic who killed him. It later turned out that this Nenad Djordjevic was close to Zoran Djindjic and that was indeed proven to be true after the takeover in October 2000. Nobody, however, prosecuted him. This Nenad Djordjevic, known as Kundak, was very prominent in that regime.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The speaker has to slow down, both of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Again, look at the transcript. Interpreters. So, Mr. Seselj, you say for a number of reasons, which include not knowing two of these persons or knowing them only for a relatively short time in terms of the relevant times in the paragraph or because of your political opposition to some of them, the allegation in paragraph 7 is untrue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It is impossible that I should belong to any sort of joint enterprise with these people, especially criminal. It leaves only Arkan with whom I was constantly in conflict, and I was the only politician in Belgrade who was not afraid of always attacking Arkan publicly. And when I appeared in court, he withdrew his charges against me. He didn't dare appear in court. And that was -- he was a very dangerous man at the time. It's simply improbable that we were all enumerated here as a group that had a common plan, common project, common enterprise. We spent much more energy on our internal conflicts and clashes than we had to spend on any sort of cooperation between any two of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And of course Mr. Milosevic didn't deal with himself, but you were in political opposition to Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. There was only one period of intense cooperation from March or April 1993 until September 1993. After the elections in December 1992, Milosevic's party was the strongest in nominal terms, but it didn't have majority in the parliament. The second largest one was the Serbian Radical Party. Milosevic's party offered to form a coalition with us, and in the headquarters of the Socialist Party the Prime Minister designate Nikola Sainovic offered us to become part of the government. I as president of the Radical Party refused it. I said it's impossible because we are ideological opponents. However, we can give you a chance. We can support a minority government for a while and if we are not happy later, we will topple it. We supported that minority government of Sainovic for about six months, after which we moved to topple it and that led to the fiercest conflict ever between the Serbian Radical Party and Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In these assassinations, Mr. Seselj, of people such as Badza, Zoran Todorovic, Bosko Perosevic, Zika Petrovic, general director of Yugoslav airlines, I don't want to forget any of them --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pavle Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Pavle Bulatovic, minister of defence. It was mainly my political friends and sympathisers that were killed.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Although we have to say about Badza that he was involved in some tobacco smuggling with a man called Cane Zabac, but this Cane Zabac was a close associate of Zoran Djindjic for whom he organised various plane trips to Arab Emirates to celebrate the new year. Cane Zabac was one of his main financiers. By some lapse of attention, probably, this -- Badza got involved with Cane Zabac, and at one point he must have gotten in his way when the latter ordered his liquidation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The next person on this list is Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan. But I believe you have provided sufficient explanation about that already. If you don't think you have said enough about your relationship with him, you can add to what you said yesterday about Arkan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You have said enough.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you feel it's enough, I won't insist. I spoke most about him while he was alive. Now that he's dead, I don't really feel comfortable talking about it but I do have to for the sake of the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We have evidence of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, when you look at this entire list, Mr. Seselj, it's in paragraph 7, it follows that some of these alleged participants in the joint criminal enterprise with whom you are joined in this paragraph are people you had never met, and with some of them you were in constant conflict.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: And with some occasionally in conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, with some occasionally in conflict. Some of them have been accused of certain crimes. I won't go into that. Some not. Do you have any explanation for this?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this was drawn up off the top of somebody's head and is not grounded in any facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not going to allow that. It can't help the trial to have the witness explain why a particular person was charged with a crime. That's not helping the case. So ask another question, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In connection with Arkan, you mentioned Dolanc.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And he was one of the most powerful people in Tito's time. After Tito's death, he was still one of the most powerful people around.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let us now move on from the topic of Arkan which you explained yesterday. You attacked Dolanc in public more than once?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In tabs 9, 10, and 11 there are excerpts from your book, "The Campaign Against Heretics," in which, would you please just take a look, you published letters which you sent to the federal public prosecutor of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were also two open letters to Dolanc.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Two open letters to Dolanc and one letter to the federal public prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The first open letter sent to Dolanc, it says: "To Stane Dolanc, member of the Presidency of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia." The second letter also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, do we need to go as far back as 1987? What is the next letter dated?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, we don't. I simply wanted to link this up, because Mr. Seselj was talking about the role of Dolanc, from that time the role of Arkan in connection with Dolanc's activities and his personal conflict and attempt to have Dolanc held responsible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can understand, your point is that in Dolanc's time Arkan became an untouchable criminal figure in Belgrade and all of the former Yugoslavia. He was really so powerful, so strong financially that one could do anything about him. I remember a detail. In 1993, I learned that Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, had in Belgrade kidnapped and taken to Erdut and there killed Isa Lero. Isa Lero was also a man from the criminal underground who had come into conflict with Arkan. I even found a witness to the murder. I publicly accused Arkan. I submitted a report to the police. The police inspectors came to see me. We talked about it. I gave them all the information I had, but then the police inspector told me that they were aware of it but that they were unable to prove it because of the fear among the potential witnesses. So the police was quite well-informed about his criminal activities, but it was very hard to prove anything or to bring charges because his support network was so widespread, and this can be shown through various newspaper articles and so on. In one television statement, I told him when we were debating on TV, that he had pulled a sock over his head more often than I had pulled one on my feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We don't need all those details.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, commenting on the questions that have to do with these alleged members of the so-called joint criminal enterprise that Mr. Nice is insisting on, you explained, when talking of your relations with Milan Babic, something about the Vance Plan pursuant to which the Blue Helmets arrived in the Krajina. Tell us, as you were very actively involved in all this, you were supporting Babic at the time and you were very familiar in great details with all the activities taking place in this connection, pursuant to the Vance Plan the Security Council established the UNPROFOR for, the UN protection force. That is not in dispute. Based on what you know and the situation on the ground or, rather, what you know about the situation on the ground, who were these forces supposed to protect and from whom?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: These forces deployed on the territory of the Republic of Serbian Krajina were supposed to defend the Serbian population from the Croatian authorities. When this plan was established, the Serb army was disarmed. Its weapons were put into depots with a double lock. One key was in the keeping of the Serbian army of the Serbian Krajina, and the other was in the keeping of UNPROFOR officers. The Vance Plan did not pre-judge a political solution to the problem. The problems remained to be solved through negotiations involving all the interested parties, primarily the political representatives of the Serbs from the Krajina and the political representatives of the Serbs from Croatia, but since the UN troops had taken control over the area and guaranteed security for the Serb population, in spite of this the Croatian forces brutally trampled on the agreement, attacked the Serb population, taking areas such as the Miljevac Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. plateau and so on and so forth. The United Nations and the Western forces unfortunately tolerated this. Ultimately, the Croats wages an aggression first against one part and then another part of the Krajina in spite of the fact that UN forces were still there causing an exodus of the entire Serb population and killing many civilians, many women, children, and elderly people. Unfortunately, only General Gotovina and some others have been indicted here. The main perpetrators have never been indicted. And this was the biggest exodus in Europe and it's still going on. The Serb population still has not returned. Either they have nowhere to return to or they don't dare return.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, you will recall and I believe that Lord Owen started this here and wrote about it in his book, he called the attack on the Krajina the greatest ethnic cleansing during the conflict in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is correct. However, the Americans through the Pentagon took a direct part in this ethnic cleansing. As you know, the Pentagon has a very powerful company which is formerly a private company but under its direct control. It's called Military Professional Resource more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: MPRI?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: MPRI, yes. That's the name of this company which employs pensioned generals, retired generals and officers to go throughout the world where the American army is avoiding direct involvement. During the attack on the Republika Srpska Krajina, the American ambassador in Zagreb Peter Galbraith stood on a Serb tank killing Serb -- on a Croatian tank killing Serb civilians. And this could be seen on television, Peter Galbraith in action.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's leave this aside for a moment. Is it clear to you how it was possible for a plan like that which was well known, it must have been well known. In the case of Operation Flash, I presented here a stenogram I received from Mr. Nice where you could see how they were preparing, how they were staging an attack, where there is evidence that there was a criminal plan to kill and expel the Serbs. What is your explanation that only one general is indicted for this?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: To avoid punishing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. Not allowed. Not allowed. He can't give any useful answer to that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice could probably give us a response, and he will have to at some point, and Madam Del Ponte. Not everyone listening to this is an idiot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic. Mr. Milosevic, you are to proceed with your questions. If you have no more questions, we will stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think that last point ought to be addressed. Again, there's no question of either myself or the Prosecutor Madam Del Ponte, being obliged to answer questions of that kind coming from the accused. It's irrelevant to the matter of this inquiry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Perhaps he was referring to your closing address but never mind. We have two more minutes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't mean that. I just wanted to express my conviction that Mr. Nice is labouring under the illusion that he will not be held criminally responsible for the crime he is perpetrating here. Not before your Bench, of course, but he will because he is one of the criminals who --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I'm going to stop on that on that -- I'm going to stop on that note. That comment is entirely inappropriate and totally without any base or foundation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I've stopped. We will adjourn for today.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before you conclude --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My right and your obligation to inform you of the following --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What are you informing me of? Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. This is a completely different matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... matter?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe it is, and it has to do with the hearing held here about Greater Serbia and Mr. Nice's standpoints and his explanations and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not going to hear anything of that. We are adjourned until 9.00 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Sorry. We are adjourned until Tuesday of next week. Tuesday of next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 30th day of August, 2005, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.43 p.m.,
